title: Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications
authors: Ion Stoica, Robert Morris, David R. Karger, M. Frans Kaashoek, Hari Balakrishnan
why_needed: Ring-topology DHT with O(log n) hops via exponentially-spaced finger table; the comparison baseline every later structured overlay (Koorde, Symphony, Viceroy, Skip+) states its own hop/state tradeoff against.

title: Pastry: Scalable, Decentralized Object Location, and Routing for Large-Scale Peer-to-Peer Systems
authors: Antony Rowstron, Peter Druschel
why_needed: Prefix-matching routing plus a defined proximity neighbor selection procedure; needed to compare prefix routing against Kademlia's XOR routing and to source the original PNS mechanism definition.

title: Tapestry: A Resilient Global-Scale Overlay for Service Deployment
authors: Ben Y. Zhao, Ling Huang, Jeremy Stribling, Sean C. Rhea, Anthony D. Joseph, John Kubiatowicz
venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
why_needed: Prefix-routing overlay with explicit fault-tolerant redundant-root replication for churn resilience; the journal version states the resilience mechanisms only sketched in the 2001 tech report.

title: A Scalable Content-Addressable Network
authors: Sylvia Ratnasamy, Paul Francis, Mark Handley, Richard Karp, Scott Shenker
why_needed: d-dimensional coordinate-space routing, the structural opposite of ring/prefix/XOR routing; needed as the fourth routing-geometry family in the geometry-comparison analysis.

title: Koorde: A Simple Degree-Optimal Distributed Hash Table
authors: M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger
why_needed: States the routing-table-size-versus-hop-count Pareto boundary directly (2 contacts at O(log n) hops, or O(log n) contacts at O(log n / log log n) hops) via a de Bruijn graph construction; the number every 'is Kademlia's k near-optimal' claim must be checked against.

title: Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly
authors: Dahlia Malkhi, Moni Naor, David Ratajczak
why_needed: Constant expected degree (7) with O(log n) hops via a butterfly-network emulation, and a proof that node join/leave costs a constant number of link changes in expectation; the fixed-degree alternative to Kademlia's O(log n)-sized k-buckets.

title: Symphony: Distributed Hashing in a Small World
authors: Gurmeet Singh Manku, Mayank Bawa, Prabhakar Raghavan
venue: USENIX Symposium on Internet Technologies and Systems
why_needed: Ring topology with k long-range links per node drawn from a harmonic (Kleinberg small-world) distribution, giving O(log^2 n / k) expected hops for an explicit, adjustable per-node link budget k; the tunable-state-versus-hop-count point against Kademlia's fixed k.

title: A Performance vs. Cost Framework for Evaluating DHT Design Tradeoffs Under Churn
authors: Jinyang Li, Jeremy Stribling, Robert Morris, M. Frans Kaashoek, Thomer M. Gil
why_needed: Introduces Accordion's self-tuning bandwidth-budget DHT (routing-table density inversely proportional to identifier distance) and the PVC (performance-vs-cost) simulation framework used to compare Chord, Kademlia, Tapestry, and other DHTs under a common churn model at a matched bandwidth budget rather than a matched table size.

title: Handling Churn in a DHT
authors: Sean Rhea, Dennis Geels, Timothy Roscoe, John Kubiatowicz
why_needed: Introduces Bamboo; isolates three independent design choices (reactive vs. periodic recovery, TCP-style adaptive timeout, proximity neighbor selection) and measures each one's separate contribution to lookup consistency under Kazaa-derived churn rates, which is the source paper the already-read HSkip+/PNS claims trace back to.

title: Efficient Routing for Peer-to-Peer Overlays
authors: Anjali Gupta, Barbara Liskov, Rodrigo Rodrigues
why_needed: One-hop DHT design: every node maintains a proactively-updated full routing table so any lookup completes in one hop, at O(n) per-node maintenance state and bandwidth; the opposite end of the hop-count-vs-state Pareto frontier from Koorde's 2-contact minimum.

title: Democratizing Content Publication with Coral
authors: Michael J. Freedman, Eric Freudenthal, David Mazieres
why_needed: A structured overlay (Coral, a hierarchical DSHT) whose lookup step optimizes for round-trip-time-measured network proximity over identifier closeness and uses sloppy (rate-limited, multi-valued) hashing rather than exact key-to-node mapping; a candidate for the brief's request for a design that departs from the pure identifier-closeness routing premise.

title: Kelips: Building an Efficient and Stable P2P DHT through Increased Memory and Background Overhead
authors: Indranil Gupta, Kenneth P. Birman, Prakash Linga, Alan J. Demers, Robbert van Renesse
why_needed: Replaces incremental identifier-closeness forwarding with O(sqrt(n))-sized affinity groups maintained by continuous background gossip, giving O(1) expected lookup hops at O(sqrt(n)) per-node state and a steady background bandwidth cost instead of an on-demand routing cost; the clearest published example of abandoning multi-hop identifier-closeness routing while keeping a structured (hash-partitioned) design.

title: Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks
authors: Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Ayalvadi Ganesh, Antony Rowstron, Dan S. Wallach
why_needed: Defines certified identifier assignment, redundant routing along disjoint paths, and a routing-failure test as the three-part defense against routing-table poisoning; the direct predecessor of S/Kademlia's disjoint-path defense that the already-read S/Kademlia paper's P_K success formula builds on.

title: Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables
authors: Emil Sit, Robert Morris
why_needed: First taxonomy of DHT-specific attack classes (routing-table corruption, storage denial, message-content corruption, network partition, and Sybil identity generation), stated independently of any one overlay's defense; needed as the classification scheme the later attack papers in this list are measured against.

title: A Survey of DHT Security Techniques
authors: Guido Urdaneta, Guillaume Pierre, Maarten van Steen
why_needed: Named by the governing brief (section 4.4) as one of the densest bibliographies to mine for the DHT attack literature; needed for its own classification of Sybil, eclipse, and routing/storage defenses and for backward-mining every defense paper it cites that this list has not already captured.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses
authors: Atul Singh, Tsuen-Wan Ngan, Peter Druschel, Dan S. Wallach
why_needed: States the eclipse attack as filling a victim's entire routing table with colluding nodes so all traffic passes through the attacker, and measures a connectivity-anonymous-auditing defense against it on a real DHT deployment; the origin measurement the term 'eclipse attack' is cited to across the entire field.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network
authors: Ethan Heilman, Alison Kendler, Aviv Zohar, Sharon Goldberg
why_needed: Demonstrates identity-forgery-based eclipse of a deployed peer-to-peer network's connection table (not DHT routing-table poisoning, since Bitcoin's network is unstructured, but the same identity-forgery mechanism the brief asks for on routing tables) and states the countermeasures (deterministic random eviction, feeler connections) later adopted into Bitcoin Core.

title: Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network
authors: Yuval Marcus, Ethan Heilman, Sharon Goldberg
why_needed: Eclipses Ethereum's Kademlia-derived node-discovery table using only a small number of attacker-controlled IP addresses, exploiting the eviction policy of the pre-discv5 Kademlia table implementation; the deployed-Kademlia identity-forgery attack the newer discv5 measurement papers (Krol, Li) state their improvement against.

title: DISC-NG: Robust Service Discovery in the Ethereum Global Network
authors: Michal Krol, Onur Ascigil, Sergi Rene, Alberto Sonnino, Matthieu Pigaglio, Ramin Sadre, Felix Lange, Etienne Riviere
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)
why_needed: Measures discv5 (Ethereum's current Kademlia-based discovery protocol) as eclipsable at a stated rate and a plain unstructured DHT walk as eclipsable at a stated higher rate, then proposes a pseudo-random advertisement-placement mechanism deployed in devp2p that lowers it; both figures need their attacker-resource and node-count conditions extracted from the full text before being cited, not the search-snippet numbers already seen (17.8%, 59.7%).

title: A Place for Everyone vs Everyone in its Place: Measuring and Attacking the Ethereum Global Network
authors: Chenyu Li, Ren Zhang, Xiaorui Gong
why_needed: Independent 2025 crawl-based measurement of discv5 network size and connectivity, plus a stated attack; deployed-DHT measurement squarely in the 2020-2026 window the brief asks this domain to prioritize, and a check on whether Krol et al.'s eclipse-rate figures replicate under a different measurement methodology.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network
authors: Ruisheng Shi, Yuxuan Liang, Zijun Guo, Qin Wang, Lina Lan, Chenfeng Wang, Zhuoyi Zheng
why_needed: 2026 eclipse-attack result on the Ethereum peer-to-peer network, published after DISC-NG's proposed defense; the forward-mining catch the brief warns a superseded 2021-era result would otherwise miss — determine on retrieval whether it attacks discv5 directly, DISC-NG, or a different layer, and whether DISC-NG's defense holds against it.

title: Understanding Churn in Peer-to-Peer Networks
authors: Daniel Stutzbach, Reza Rejaie
why_needed: Measures session-length distributions on three deployed peer-to-peer networks (not derived from any one DHT's own logs) and shows median session length is a misleading summary because the distribution is heavy-tailed; the churn-rate input every structured-overlay churn-resilience claim (Bamboo, HSkip+) needs a stated real distribution for, rather than an assumed Poisson or exponential model.

title: The Impact of DHT Routing Geometry on Resilience and Proximity
authors: Krishna P. Gummadi, Ramakrishna Gummadi, Steven D. Gribble, Sylvia Ratnasamy, Scott Shenker, Ion Stoica
why_needed: Isolates routing geometry (tree/hypercube/ring/butterfly/XOR) as a variable independent of any single protocol and shows which geometries permit choosing among multiple next-hop candidates at each forwarding step (a prerequisite for both proximity neighbor selection and disjoint-path routing); the paper the already-read S/Kademlia paper's claim about XOR's routing flexibility ultimately traces to.

title: A Global View of KAD
authors: Moritz Steiner, Taoufik En-Najjary, Ernst W. Biersack
why_needed: Large-scale crawl of KAD, the Kademlia-derived DHT deployed in eMule/eDonkey, giving directly measured routing-table staleness, churn, and lookup behavior on a real Kademlia deployment at a scale the original Kademlia paper's simulation did not reach; a baseline the 2020s IPFS/Ethereum Kademlia measurements can be compared against for whether deployed-Kademlia behavior changed over 15+ years.

title: Exploiting KAD: Possible Uses and Misuses
authors: Moritz Steiner, Taoufik En-Najjary, Ernst W. Biersack
why_needed: States concrete attacks against the deployed KAD Kademlia network (routing-table poisoning, publish/retrieve denial, identity-forgery-based eclipse) executed against the live network from the same crawl infrastructure as the companion measurement paper, with the resource cost of each attack stated; a directly measured cost figure to set against Sybil/eclipse cost claims made only in simulation.

title: R/Kademlia: Recursive and Topology-aware Overlay Routing
authors: Bernhard Heep
venue: Australasian Telecommunication Networks and Applications Conference (ATNAC)
why_needed: Recursive-routing variant of Kademlia combined with proximity routing and proximity neighbor selection, stated as lower-latency under KAD-characteristic churn than iterative Kademlia; the direct recursive-vs-iterative comparison paper for the brief's explicit 'iterative versus recursive routing' subtopic, since the original Kademlia paper only argues for iterative routing without measuring against a recursive variant.

title: SKIP+: A Self-Stabilizing Skip Graph
authors: Riko Jacob, Andrea W. Richa, Christian Scheideler, Stefan Schmid, Hanjo Taubig
why_needed: Proves a distributed algorithm that restores a valid skip graph from any weakly-connected state in polylogarithmic time without external intervention; the self-stabilization result the already-read HSkip+ paper's own self-stabilization proof is built directly on top of, needed to separate what HSkip+ itself proved from what it inherited from this paper.

title: Survey on Algorithms for Self-Stabilizing Overlay Networks
authors: Michael Feldmann, Christian Scheideler, Stefan Schmid
why_needed: Found by forward-mining the already-read HSkip+ paper's citation list; the unified survey of the self-stabilizing-overlay literature (Skip+, HSkip+, and the lines that came after both), needed to check whether a design published after 2014 dominates HSkip+ on the same bandwidth-heterogeneity property before any selection is made.

title: IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide
authors: Dennis Trautwein, Yiluo Wei, Yiannis Psaras, Moritz Schubotz, Ignacio Castro, Bela Gipp, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: Measures Kademlia record-publish latency on the live IPFS DHT and states an optimistic-provide protocol change; a prior research pass in this project already cited specific latency percentiles (6.3s median, 20.6s p90, 49.8s p95) from this paper by title, and rule 1 requires those numbers re-extracted from the full text with their exact measurement conditions (node count, geographic distribution, DHT client version) before any later document may state them again.

title: The Eternal Tussle: Exploring the Role of Centralization in IPFS
authors: Yiluo Wei, Dennis Trautwein, Yiannis Psaras, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: Measures how much of IPFS content-location traffic passes through a small number of centralized indexing and gateway services versus the Kademlia DHT itself; the 2024 update to the centralization-measurement literature the brief's already-summarized 2024 Wei et al. NSDI finding (one centralized indexer holding over 100x the DHT's location records) needs verified from full text before being restated with a number attached.

title: The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS
authors: Leonhard Balduf, Maciej Korczynski, Onur Ascigil, Navin V. Keizer, George Pavlou, Bjorn Scheuermann, Michal Krol
why_needed: A second, independent 2023 measurement of IPFS centralization from a different author group than Wei et al. 2024; the brief requires presenting disagreeing measurements of the same system side by side with conditions stated, so both papers must be extracted even where their headline claims agree, to check whether their measurement methodologies and time windows actually agree too.

title: Centralization in the Decentralized Web: Challenges and Opportunities in IPFS Data Management
authors: Ruizhe Shi, Ruizhi Cheng, Yuqi Fu, Bo Han, Yue Cheng, Songqing Chen
why_needed: A third, 2025 independent measurement of IPFS data replication and centralization (stated in search results as approximately 2.71% of files replicated more than 5 times); a third data point against Balduf 2023 and Wei 2024 needed to determine whether IPFS centralization is worsening, stable, or measured differently by each group before any trend claim is stated in the synthesis.

title: Kadabra: Adapting Kademlia for the Decentralized Web
authors: Yunqi Zhang, Shaileshh Bojja Venkatakrishnan
why_needed: Proposes and states a measured lookup-latency and load-balance change to Kademlia specifically for content-addressed decentralized-web workloads (as opposed to the file-sharing workload Kademlia and KAD were designed and measured for); tests whether Kademlia's original design assumptions hold for a workload closer to the one this architecture targets.

title: Scalability Limitations of Kademlia DHTs when Enabling Data Availability Sampling in Ethereum
authors: Mikel Cortes-Goicoechea, Csaba Kiraly, Dmitriy Ryajov, Jose Luis Munoz-Tapia, Leonardo Bautista-Gomez
why_needed: Measures Kademlia lookup latency and success rate under a specific high-query-rate workload (data availability sampling) at Ethereum-consensus-layer node counts; a stated case where a workload characteristic (query rate rather than churn) is the limiting factor on Kademlia performance, distinct from every churn-focused measurement already in this list.

title: On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search
authors: Jinyang Li, Boon Thau Loo, Joseph M. Hellerstein, M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger, Robert Morris
why_needed: States the standing feasibility bound for word-partitioned distributed full-text search at web scale (query broadcast vs. DHT posting-list intersection, Bloom-filter intersection, caching, precomputation). Open problem 1 in the brief asks whether this bound has been overturned; every later target in this list that touches distributed inverted indexes must be checked against this paper's stated cost model and assumptions before any claim of improvement is accepted.

title: On the Feasibility of Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Information Retrieval
authors: H. Asthana, Ruoxun Fu, Ingemar J. Cox
venue: ICTIR (Int. Conf. on the Theory of Information Retrieval)
why_needed: This is the 2011 ICTIR paper the prior pass attributed a '6 MB per query, 3 billion documents' figure to as a follow-up of Li et al. (rule-1 violation risk: prior pass's own corpus notes this figure needs re-verification against primary text). Applies a probably-approximately-correct (PAC) search framework, distinct from Li et al.'s posting-list-cost model, to the same feasibility question, and derives peer-contact counts under uniform, proportional, and square-root document distributions -- a second, independent route to an unstructured-search feasibility bound that must be read before either number is cited.

title: Probably Approximately Correct Search
authors: Ingemar J. Cox, Ruoxun Fu, Lars Kai Hansen
why_needed: Introduces the PAC (probably-approximately-correct) search framework -- the theoretical machinery Asthana et al. (ICTIR 2011) extend to unstructured P2P networks. Needed to separate what is proved about centralized PAC search from what changes when the framework is transplanted to a P2P setting, since the P2P paper's guarantees depend on assumptions stated only here.

title: Improving Query Correctness Using Centralized Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Search
authors: Ingemar J. Cox, Jianhan Zhu, Ruoxun Fu, Lars Kai Hansen
why_needed: Second step in the PAC-search line, still centralized, refining the accuracy guarantee later carried into the P2P feasibility analysis. Needed to trace which PAC guarantee changed between the centralized and the distributed versions of the framework.

title: Ranked Accuracy and Unstructured Distributed Search
authors: Sami Richardson, Ingemar J. Cox
why_needed: Defines a rank-weighted accuracy metric for unstructured distributed search (as opposed to the binary found/not-found metric used by Li et al. and Lv et al.) and measures a 10,000-node simulation against it. Needed because square-root replication and the PAC bound are both stated in terms of a binary search-success criterion; this paper's metric may change what 'search cost' means for a ranked-retrieval architecture.

title: Increasing Ranked Accuracy for Unstructured Distributed Search with Dynamic Replication
authors: Sami Richardson, Ingemar J. Cox
why_needed: Adds a dynamic-replication scheme aimed directly at the ranked-accuracy metric from Richardson & Cox (ECIR 2013). Directly relevant to the brief's known incompatibility between square-root replication (which needs to know which item a search found) and a search channel that returns only match/no-match -- this paper's replication trigger must be checked for the same dependency.

title: Estimating Global Statistics for Unstructured P2P Search in the Presence of Adversarial Peers
authors: Sami Richardson, Ingemar J. Cox
why_needed: Explicit adversarial analysis of the PAC/unstructured-search line: measures what happens to global-statistics estimation (needed for ranking and replication decisions) when some peers are adversarial. This is the concrete failure-condition source for anything in this line the synthesis wants to select under a non-benign threat model.

title: PAC'nPost: A Peer-to-Peer Micro-blogging Social Network
authors: Harshvardhan Asthana
why_needed: Expanded, full-length version of the PAC'nPost application-layer design that the WWW 2012 paper states in only two pages; contains the PAC-search-based microblog publish/follow/search mechanism and its evaluation in full. Needed because a two-page poster cannot state the mechanism in implementable detail, and the brief's protocol specifically calls for retrieving an author's thesis when the conference version is too short.

title: On Unstructured Distributed Search over BitTorrent
authors: William Mayor, Ingemar J. Cox
why_needed: Tests the unstructured/PAC-search line against a real deployed network (BitTorrent) rather than a simulation, evaluating an unstructured discovery mechanism as a censorship-resistant fallback when centralized trackers or the Mainline DHT are unavailable. Needed as the one entry in this lineage measured against live network conditions rather than a synthetic topology.

title: OverCite: A Cooperative Digital Research Library
authors: Jeremy Stribling, Isaac G. Councill, Jinyang Li, M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger, Robert Morris, Scott Shenker
why_needed: This is the 'Alvis, also called OverCite' system the domain description names: a full-text academic-citation index (CiteSeer's corpus) partitioned and replicated over a DHT using a three-tier design (presentation servers, application/index servers, DHT storage). Needed to state the mechanism by which a large existing index was actually distributed across untrusted-capacity peers, as a concrete precedent for term/document partitioning at a scale larger than a lab simulation.

title: Replication Strategies in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks
authors: Edith Cohen, Scott Shenker
why_needed: Proves the square-root-replication optimality result (uniform and proportional replication give identical average search size m/rho independent of query distribution; replication proportional to sqrt(query rate) minimizes it) that Lv et al. (already read) implement via path replication. The brief's already-read summary of Lv et al. attributes the analytic optimality claim to 'Cohen and Shenker'; this is that paper, and it has not itself been read yet -- needed to check whether the analytic proof carries assumptions (e.g., on replica lifetime independence) not visible in the Lv et al. implementation paper.

title: Mapping the Gnutella Network: Properties of Large-Scale Peer-to-Peer Systems and Implications for System Design
authors: Matei Ripeanu, Ian T. Foster, Adriana Iamnitchi
why_needed: Direct measurement of the deployed Gnutella query-broadcast network's topology and traffic, cited by the prior-pass corpus as the empirical motivation for the two-tier / supernode response to flooding cost. Needed as the primary source for that claim rather than the secondary paraphrase in the prior pass.

title: A Measurement Study of Napster and Gnutella as Examples of Peer-to-Peer File Sharing Systems
authors: P. Krishna Gummadi, Stefan Saroiu, Steven D. Gribble
why_needed: Independent measurement of end-host heterogeneity (bandwidth, availability, and content-sharing behavior) in two deployed unstructured networks. This is the measurement most directly cited as the reason a flat unstructured overlay is replaced by a capacity-ordered two-tier design (Yang & Garcia-Molina); needed to state the actual heterogeneity distribution rather than assert the design response as self-evident.

title: Designing a Super-Peer Network
authors: Beverly Yang, Hector Garcia-Molina
why_needed: States the mechanism and the design parameters (fan-out, index-forwarding vs. query-forwarding, super-peer-to-super-peer topology) for the two-tier response to flat query broadcast named in the domain description. Needed to extract the actual cost tradeoffs the design makes, rather than treat 'two-tier' as a label.

title: Optimal Aggregation Algorithms for Middleware
authors: Ronald Fagin, Amnon Lotem, Moni Naor
venue: ACM PODS (journal version: J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 66, 2003)
why_needed: Defines the Threshold Algorithm (TA) and proves its instance-optimality for top-k aggregation over multiple sorted/random-access lists -- the threshold-algorithm family the domain description names by Fagin's name. This is the primitive that any distributed top-k retrieval scheme (e.g., Michel et al.'s KLEE) implements over a network of partial result lists; needed before any distributed top-k claim can be checked against the algorithm it is built on.

title: Semantic Overlay Networks for P2P Systems
authors: Arturo Crespo, Hector Garcia-Molina
why_needed: States the mechanism for a Semantic Overlay Network (SON): peers connect preferentially to others holding similar content, and queries route first within the matching SON rather than broadcasting network-wide. This is the named foundational construction behind every later interest-based/semantic overlay (including 4P and Semantica, already or newly in this list) and needed to check what each later paper actually changes relative to it.

title: pSearch: Information Retrieval in Structured Overlays
authors: Chunqiang Tang, Zhichen Xu, Mallik Mahalingam
why_needed: Places document vectors (via Latent Semantic Indexing) onto a structured overlay (CAN) so that semantically similar documents map to nearby coordinates, letting a query route directly to the region holding relevant documents instead of broadcasting or maintaining a global inverted index. This is a structurally different answer to distributed full-text/semantic retrieval than the unstructured-overlay and inverted-index lines above, and needed as the comparison point for cost and recall.

title: Efficient Peer-to-Peer Keyword Searching
authors: Patrick Reynolds, Amin Vahdat
why_needed: States a concrete distributed-inverted-index design over a DHT using Bloom filters, caching, and incremental results to reduce the bandwidth of multi-keyword intersection -- the specific Bloom-filter-intersection mechanism the domain description names alongside term/document partitioning and threshold algorithms. Needed to extract the actual bandwidth and latency figures under stated conditions, for direct comparison against Li et al.'s feasibility bound.

title: The Case for a Hybrid P2P Search Infrastructure
authors: Boon Thau Loo, Ryan Huebsch, Ion Stoica, Joseph M. Hellerstein
why_needed: Written by an overlapping author set to Li et al.'s feasibility paper, this argues that flooding suits popular (highly replicated) items while a structured DHT suits rare items, and proposes combining both rather than picking one -- a direct architectural response to the feasibility bound. Needed to check whether this hybrid actually escapes the ~6 MB-per-query cost class or only relocates it.

title: BubbleStorm: Resilient, Probabilistic, and Exhaustive Peer-to-Peer Search
authors: Wesley W. Terpstra, Jussi Kangasharju, Christof Leng, Alejandro P. Buchmann
why_needed: States a random-multigraph replication/search scheme with a stated probabilistic exhaustiveness guarantee (every matching item found with a stated probability), evaluated at one million simulated peers under up to 90% simultaneous departure and 50% simultaneous crash. This is a different cost/guarantee tradeoff than the k-walker random walk (Lv et al., already read) or query broadcast, and needed as the comparison point for exhaustive-search cost under churn.

title: KLEE: A Framework for Distributed Top-k Query Algorithms
authors: Sebastian Michel, Peter Triantafillou, Gerhard Weikum
why_needed: Implements Fagin-style threshold-algorithm top-k aggregation over a DHT-distributed network rather than a single machine's sorted lists, by the same author group as MINERVA (already read). Needed to state exactly how a threshold algorithm's random-access and sorted-access assumptions are realized (or relaxed) once the lists live on different, unreliable peers.

title: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs
authors: Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin
venue: IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 42(4) (preprint arXiv:1603.09320, 2016)
why_needed: States the HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) mechanism the domain description names: a multi-layer proximity graph searched greedily from the top layer down, giving logarithmic-scaling approximate nearest-neighbor search. This is the graph-based ANN index every distribution-across-untrusted-peers proposal (open problem 2) must be checked against for what its greedy-routing invariant requires from the storage layer.

title: Product Quantization for Nearest Neighbor Search
authors: Herve Jegou, Matthijs Douze, Cordelia Schmid
venue: IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 33(1)
why_needed: States the product-quantization mechanism underlying IVF-PQ (Inverted File with Product Quantization), the domain description's second named vector-index family: partitions vector space into a Cartesian product of subspaces and quantizes each independently, compressing each vector to a short code while supporting asymmetric distance estimation. Needed as the compression-and-partition baseline against which any distributed or bandwidth-constrained vector index is compared.

title: Rand-NSG: Fast Accurate Billion-point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node
authors: Suhas Jayaram Subramanya, Devvrit, Harsha Vardhan Simhadri, Ravishankar Krishnaswamy, Rohan Kadekodi
why_needed: This is the paper that introduced the DiskANN mechanism (indexed in DBLP under its algorithm name Rand-NSG): a single-shot graph-construction algorithm (alpha-pruning) letting a billion-point ANN graph index be searched mostly from SSD rather than RAM. Named directly in the domain description; needed as the baseline single-machine mechanism before evaluating any proposal (below) to distribute it.

title: DistributedANN: Efficient Scaling of a Single DiskANN Graph Across Thousands of Computers
authors: Philip Adams, Menghao Li, Shi Zhang, Li Tan, Qi Chen, Mingqin Li, Zengzhong Li, Knut Magne Risvik, Harsha Vardhan Simhadri
why_needed: Current (2025) state of the art for scaling a single DiskANN graph index across many machines, superseding single-node DiskANN (Subramanya et al., 2019) on the scaling axis. Directly answers half of open problem 2 (distributing an ANN index across many participants) but under a managed/trusted-cluster model, not an adversarial-peer model -- needed to state precisely which assumptions (participant identity, no data corruption, coordinated placement) would have to be relaxed for a decentralized, untrusted-participant setting, since the paper does not itself address that threat model.

title: Poisoning Retrieval Corpora by Injecting Adversarial Passages
authors: Zexuan Zhong, Ziqing Huang, Alexander Wettig, Danqi Chen
why_needed: States a gradient-based (HotFlip-style) method for crafting a small number of adversarial passages that a dense retriever ranks highly for many unrelated queries, when injected into the retrieval corpus. This is the foundational corpus-poisoning attack on dense/vector retrieval directly answering the domain's call for 'adversarial-vector and poisoning attacks on ANN indexes' -- needed to state the attack's cost (how many injected passages, how much query-set knowledge) as a fact before any defense claim is evaluated against it.

title: Unsupervised Corpus Poisoning Attacks in Continuous Space for Dense Retrieval
authors: Yongkang Li, Panagiotis Eustratiadis, Simon Lupart, Evangelos Kanoulas
why_needed: Follow-on corpus-poisoning attack that removes the query-supervision requirement of Zhong et al. (2023), operating directly in the retriever's continuous embedding space. Needed to check whether removing that requirement changes the attack's cost or detectability, since the two papers' threat models differ and both are needed to state the full attack-cost range for the synthesis's threat-model comparison.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Adversarially Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
authors: Alexandr Andoni, Themistoklis Haris, Esty Kelman, Krzysztof Onak
why_needed: 2026 theoretical result giving algorithms for ANN search under an adaptive adversary that controls both the stored dataset and the query sequence, connecting robustness to a fairness property and to differentially-private mechanisms over locality-sensitive hashing. Needed because this is the freshest, most direct answer this pass found to open problem 2's request for ANN search that resists inserted adversarial vectors, and its stated model (adaptive adversary, provable guarantee) needs to be checked against what a real distributed-among-untrusted-peers deployment would actually expose.

title: Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Chenhao Xu, Longxiang Gao, Yuan Miao, Xi Zheng
why_needed: States a Topic-Aware Random Walk mechanism for peer discovery in a peer-to-peer retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) network: an LLM extracts a query's topic, and the walk is biased toward peers likely to hold topically relevant knowledge, rather than a uniform random walk. This is exactly the 2023-2026 move the domain description calls out ('decentralized retrieval-augmented generation... is where this problem moved') and is a direct descendant of the unstructured-search random-walk line (Lv et al., already read); needed to check whether topic-biasing changes the message-cost scaling that made k-walker search viable.

title: Pacmann: Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
authors: Mingxun Zhou, Elaine Shi, Giulia Fanti
why_needed: States a protocol for approximate nearest-neighbor search over an encrypted/outsourced vector database such that the server holding the index does not learn the query vector. Needed because it sits directly at the intersection the brief flags between the strongest replication/search results and privacy: any selection of HNSW or IVF-PQ for a privacy tier must be checked against what this paper's protocol requires from the index structure (e.g., whether it needs the full graph, or only cluster centroids) and what latency or bandwidth cost it states for that guarantee.

title: A Survey on Content Retrieval on the Decentralised Web
authors: Navin V. Keizer, Onur Ascigil, Michal Kral, Dirk Kutscher, George Pavlou
why_needed: 2024 Computing Surveys article covering decentralized file systems, decentralized search engines, and name-registry infrastructures together, satisfying the brief's requirement for a 2023-or-later survey/SoK in this domain. Needed as a map of which decentralized-retrieval mechanism families this pass may have missed, and as a cross-check on classification/terminology against the rest of the corpus. A companion PhD thesis by the first author ('Decentralising Content Retrieval on the Decentralised Web', UCL, discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10181270) exists in expanded form and should be pulled by the reading pass if the survey itself leaves a mechanism under-specified.

title: Censorship-Resistant and Privacy-Preserving Distributed Web Search
authors: Michael Herrmann, Ren Zhang, Kai-Chun Ning, Claudia Diaz, Bart Preneel
why_needed: Analyzes the three deployed distributed web-search engines the domain description names by name (Faroo, Seeks, and YaCy) for censorship resistance and query-privacy, and states that none provides adequate protection against a modestly resourced adversary. This is the primary academic-quality source available for YaCy and Seeks -- neither project has a peer-reviewed paper of its own describing its architecture, so this is the route to a checkable claim about either rather than an assertion from project documentation.

title: Difficulty-Aware Hybrid Search in Peer-to-Peer Networks
authors: Hanhua Chen, Hai Jin, Yunhao Liu, Lionel M. Ni
venue: IEEE Trans. Parallel Distributed Syst. 20(1) (conference precursor: ICPP 2007)
why_needed: Resolves the brief's open item 'QRank': QRank is the ranking scheme defined inside this paper (not a paper title of its own), which weights query keywords by term-frequency-derived difficulty and routes each query to an unstructured flood, a DHT lookup, or a hybrid of both depending on the estimated peer-count needed to answer it. Needed to state the actual rule this scheme uses to pick a search strategy, since the domain description names both unstructured/broadcast search and DHT-based indexing as options this kind of hybrid must choose between.

title: SwarmSearch: Decentralized Search Engine with Self-Funding Economy
authors: Marcel Gregoriadis, Rowdy Chotkan, Petru Neague, Johan Pouwelse
why_needed: 2025 successor in the same TU Delft/Tribler lineage as 4P (already read): a decentralized AI-assisted search engine that states retrieval accuracy while stating robustness under 50% adversarial nodes, plus a per-peer utility-score economic layer for sustaining volunteer resource contribution. Resolves the brief's other unresolved-citation item ('SwarmSearch'). Needed to check whether it changes the recall/message-cost tradeoff 4P reported, now under an adversarial-node condition 4P did not test.

title: Semantica: Decentralized Search using a LLM-Guided Semantic Tree Overlay
authors: Petru Neague, Quinten Stokkink, Naman Goel, Johan Pouwelse
why_needed: 2025 semantic overlay construction (same author lineage as SwarmSearch) that uses an LLM to guide placement of peers into a tree-structured semantic overlay, replacing the similarity computation Crespo & Garcia-Molina's original SON left as an open design choice. Needed as the current state of interest-based/semantic overlay construction, and as a concrete instance of an LLM in the retrieval-routing path whose failure modes (hallucinated similarity judgments, prompt-injection-style manipulation of routing) have not yet been checked against the classical semantic-overlay literature.

title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
authors: Wei Zou, Runpeng Geng, Binghui Wang, Jinyuan Jia
why_needed: States an optimization-based knowledge-corruption attack against RAG systems achieving a stated attack-success rate with as few as five injected documents in a corpus of millions, a different threat framing (attacker chooses the LLM's answer, not just which passage is retrieved) than the corpus-poisoning-of-the-retriever attacks (Zhong et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025). Needed as the RAG-generation-level attack cost distinct from the retrieval-level attack cost, since a decentralized RAG design (Xu et al., 2025, above) must defend against both.

title: Polynomial Codes Over Certain Finite Fields
authors: Irving S. Reed, Gustave Solomon
venue: Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
why_needed: Origin of Reed-Solomon codes, the maximum-distance-separable construction every later erasure-coded storage system (Storj, Sia, Xorbas, Azure LRC, Clay codes) uses or benchmarks against for the storage-overhead-versus-fault-tolerance tradeoff at overhead n/k.

title: A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function
authors: Ralph C. Merkle
why_needed: Origin of the hash tree construction underlying every content-addressed, Merkle-linked data structure (IPFS's IPLD, Git, Filecoin's sector proofs) that lets a verifier check one leaf against a small path of hashes rather than downloading the whole structure.

title: LT Codes
authors: Michael Luby
venue: IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
why_needed: First practical rateless fountain code: a sender produces an unbounded stream of coded symbols from k source symbols and any (1+epsilon)k of them suffice to decode, with no fixed rate n/k to pre-select. Foundational for Raptor and RaptorQ, and the alternative to fixed-rate Reed-Solomon for object delivery over an unreliable channel of unknown loss rate.

title: Raptor Codes
authors: Amin Shokrollahi
why_needed: Concatenates an outer fixed-rate code with an inner LT code to make decoding cost linear in k and overhead approach zero as k grows, fixing LT codes' non-linear decode cost. The basis of RaptorQ (RFC 6330) and of every fountain-code argument for encoding storage objects once and letting any sufficient subset of coded pieces reconstruct them, independent of which pieces are held by which peers.

title: RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery
authors: Michael Luby, Amin Shokrollahi, Mark Watson, Thomas Stockhammer, Lorenz Minder
why_needed: The deployed rateless-code standard: states decoding failure probability at exactly k received symbols (roughly 1%) and at k+1 or k+2 (roughly 0.01% and near-zero), and the block and sub-symbol size parameters used in production object-delivery systems. Sets the concrete failure-probability-versus-overhead curve a fountain-coded storage design should be checked against, rather than an assumed one.

title: Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems
authors: Alexandros G. Dimakis, P. Brighten Godfrey, Yunnan Wu, Martin J. Wainwright, Kannan Ramchandran
why_needed: Origin of regenerating codes: derives the storage-versus-repair-bandwidth tradeoff curve for reconstructing one lost coded piece from d helper nodes, and states the two extreme points on that curve — Minimum-Storage Regenerating (MSR, storage overhead equal to plain erasure coding, higher repair bandwidth) and Minimum-Bandwidth Regenerating (MBR, higher storage overhead, lowest possible repair bandwidth). This is the tradeoff curve every later construction (product-matrix, Clay, LRC, convertible) is checked against.

title: Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction
authors: K. V. Rashmi, Nihar B. Shah, P. Vijay Kumar
why_needed: First explicit code construction that hits both MSR and MBR points with exact repair (the repaired piece is bit-for-bit identical to the lost one, not merely functionally equivalent), for all storage-overhead parameters, at the cost of a minimum-helper-count requirement d >= 2k-1 for MSR. States that requirement explicitly, which is the exact number a liveness objection to regenerating codes (any k of n survive storage, but a repair needs d of n-1 remaining pieces simultaneously reachable) must be checked against.

title: Locally Repairable Codes
authors: Dimitris S. Papailiopoulos, Alexandros G. Dimakis
why_needed: Defines locality r: the number of other coded pieces that must be read to reconstruct one lost piece, distinct from the regenerating-code d (number of helper nodes contacted). Proves a Singleton-type bound coupling locality, minimum distance, and storage overhead, and shows locality can be small (independent of n) at a fixed storage-overhead cost. This is what a repair-liveness objection to regenerating codes (needing d of n-1 pieces live) can be traded against: lower r means fewer pieces to contact per repair, at a different overhead price than MSR/MBR.

title: Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage
authors: Cheng Huang, Huseyin Simitci, Yikang Xu, Aaron Ogus, Brad Calder, Parikshit Gopalan, Jin Li, Sergey Yekhanin
why_needed: Deployed measurement of a locally repairable code (Azure's LRC) running in production storage, reporting reconstruction I/O and repair bandwidth reduction relative to Reed-Solomon at a stated storage-overhead cost. The reference point for what locality gains look like outside a simulation, cited by nearly every later locally-repairable-code paper as its deployed baseline.

title: XORing Elephants: Novel Erasure Codes for Big Data
authors: Maheswaran Sathiamoorthy, Megasthenis Asteris, Dimitris S. Papailiopoulos, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ramkumar Vadali, Scott Chen, Dhruba Borthakur
why_needed: Deployed measurement of the Xorbas locally repairable code running on a Facebook production Hadoop cluster, reporting disk I/O and repair network traffic reduction against plain Reed-Solomon at a stated cluster scale. A second deployed data point (alongside Azure LRC) for what a locality-versus-overhead choice returns on a real repair workload, from a different operator and workload than Azure's.

title: Clay Codes: Moulding MDS Codes to Yield an MSR Code
authors: Myna Vajha, Vinayak Ramkumar, Bhagyashree Puranik, Ganesh R. Kini, Elita A. Lobo, Birenjith Sasidharan, P. Vijay Kumar, Alexander Barg, Min Ye, Srinivasan Narayanamurthy, Syed Hussain, Siddhartha Nandi
venue: USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies (FAST)
why_needed: Construction that produces a minimum-storage-regenerating code from any Maximum-Distance-Separable code by pairwise-coupling scalar values ("coupled-layer" transform), reported deployed in Ceph, with measured repair-bandwidth reduction against Reed-Solomon at production scale. Directly competes with the product-matrix construction (RASHMI-TIT-11) on the same MSR point and is the deployed alternative construction whose reported numbers the product-matrix numbers must be checked against.

title: Convertible Codes: Enabling Efficient Conversion of Coded Data in Distributed Storage
authors: Francisco Maturana, K. V. Rashmi
why_needed: Defines code conversion: changing an already-stored object's erasure-code parameters (for example raising or lowering storage overhead as durability requirements change) without a full re-encode from the original data. States the bandwidth cost of conversion as a function of the before and after parameters, which bears directly on repair economics because a repair after partial data loss is a special case of conversion (converting from a degraded to a full parameter set).

title: Locally Repairable Convertible Codes: Erasure Codes for Efficient Repair and Conversion
authors: Francisco Maturana, K. V. Rashmi
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT)
why_needed: Combines locally repairable codes and convertible codes into one construction, so repairing a lost piece and later converting the object's storage-overhead parameters both cost less than treating them as separate operations under the prior separate constructions. A 2023 result directly answering the brief's search for work lowering the resource cost of repair since the 2010-2018 regenerating/locally-repairable code line.

title: Locally Repairable Convertible Codes With Optimal Access Costs
authors: Xiangliang Kong
why_needed: An independently authored 2024 construction in the same locally-repairable-convertible-code space as MATURANA-ISIT-23, optimizing the count of pieces accessed during conversion rather than bandwidth. A second, independent construction whose optimality claims and access-cost numbers the Maturana-Rashmi line must be checked against.

title: Tight Lower Bounds and Optimal Constructions of Locally Repairable Convertible Codes in the Split Regime
authors: Haoming Shi, Weijun Fang
why_needed: June 2026 result proving a lower bound on conversion bandwidth in the split regime (one stored object's parameters split into several with different parameters) and a construction meeting it, closing a gap left open by the 2023-2025 locally-repairable-convertible-code papers. Confirms the sub-field was still moving in the two months before this pass, so any bandwidth-optimality claim taken from an earlier LRCC paper needs checking against this bound.

title: Generalized Regenerating Codes and Node Repair on Graphs
authors: Adway Patra, Alexander Barg
why_needed: Extends regenerating codes from the standard model (any d of the remaining n-1 nodes can serve as helpers, all links equal) to an arbitrary graph in which only specified nodes can communicate and links carry nonuniform capacities. Directly relevant to the repair-liveness objection to regenerating codes: it replaces the requirement 'd specific live holders reachable' with a requirement stated over whichever holders the network graph actually connects, which is a materially different and possibly weaker liveness condition depending on the graph's structure.

title: Erasure Coding Vs. Replication: A Quantitative Comparison
authors: Hakim Weatherspoon, John Kubiatowicz
why_needed: First quantitative comparison of whole-copy replication against erasure coding for a peer-to-peer storage system at matched durability, reporting the storage-overhead and repair-bandwidth cost of each at stated node-availability levels. One of two independent papers (with RODRIGUES-IPTPS-05) making this comparison; the brief requires holding both since competing papers frequently disagree on the numbers.

title: High Availability in DHTs: Erasure Coding vs. Replication
authors: Rodrigo Rodrigues, Barbara Liskov
why_needed: A second, independent replication-versus-erasure-coding comparison, run three years after WEATHERSPOON-IPTPS-02 with a distributed-hash-table-specific availability model, reporting the repair-bandwidth crossover point at which erasure coding stops being cheaper than replication as node availability drops. Holds the comparison numbers from a different research group under a different availability model, which the brief requires be checked against the first paper's numbers rather than assumed to agree.

title: High Availability, Scalable Storage, Dynamic Peer Networks: Pick Two
authors: Charles Blake, Rodrigo Rodrigues
venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS)
why_needed: Derives a lower bound on the per-node bandwidth a peer-to-peer storage system needs for repair, as a function of measured node session length (churn rate), stored data volume per node, and target durability, and shows the bound is violated by then-typical residential upload bandwidth at then-measured churn rates. The formula is the one a repair-economics claim for any erasure-coded storage design must be run through with the design's own n, k, and measured churn rate as inputs, rather than asserted qualitatively.

title: Efficient Replica Maintenance for Distributed Storage Systems
authors: Byung-Gon Chun, Frank Dabek, Andreas Haeberlen, Emil Sit, Hakim Weatherspoon, M. Frans Kaashoek, John Kubiatowicz, Robert Morris
venue: USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI)
why_needed: The Carbonite system: measures repair bandwidth on a live PlanetLab deployment under real node churn traces and shows that repairing every transient failure (as a naive scheme does) drives repair bandwidth far above the durability-necessary minimum; introduces a repair policy that defers repair for short-lived departures and reports the resulting bandwidth reduction against the naive policy on the same trace. Directly supplies the measured-churn repair-traffic figures the brief's repair-economics question requires.

title: Total Recall: System Support for Automated Availability Management
authors: Ranjita Bhagwan, Kiran Tati, Yuchung Cheng, Stefan Savage, Geoffrey M. Voelker
venue: USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI)
why_needed: System that continuously measures each node's observed availability and adjusts per-object redundancy (replication or erasure-coding rate) to a target durability, reporting the resulting repair-bandwidth cost against a fixed-redundancy baseline under a real availability trace. The paper CHUN-NSDI-06 explicitly responds to and improves on, so holding both supplies the before-and-after repair-bandwidth numbers for the same design question.

title: Understanding Availability
authors: Ranjita Bhagwan, Stefan Savage, Geoffrey M. Voelker
why_needed: Measures host availability (fraction of time online) across a large deployed peer-to-peer system (Overnet) and reports the distribution's shape and its implication for how availability should be modeled in a repair-economics calculation, as opposed to assuming a single mean availability figure. The churn-rate input BLAKE-HOTOS-03's bandwidth bound and CHUN-NSDI-06's repair-policy design both need, from a system independent of either.

title: The Computational and Storage Potential of Volunteer Computing
authors: David P. Anderson, Gilles Fedak
venue: IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Cluster Computing and the Grid (CCGrid)
why_needed: Measures disk space, availability, and churn across more than 330,000 hosts in a deployed volunteer-computing project (BOINC), reporting the aggregate storage capacity those hosts could supply and the fraction actually reachable at any moment. The direct measurement the brief's 'what does volunteer storage actually supply' question calls for, from hosts running unmodified consumer software rather than a research testbed.

title: PORs: Proofs of Retrievability for Large Files
authors: Ari Juels, Burton S. Kaliski Jr.
venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Defines proof of retrievability: a storage provider proves, via a compact challenge-response exchange, that it still holds a specific file in full, without transmitting the file. Introduces the use of embedded random-check blocks (sentinels) mixed into an erasure-coded encoding of the file so an incorrect response to a spot check statistically implies data has been altered or lost. States the security bound as a function of the fraction of the file corrupted and the number of sentinels checked.

title: Compact Proofs of Retrievability
authors: Hovav Shacham, Brent Waters
why_needed: Improves on JUELS-CCS-07 with a homomorphic authenticator construction that lets a verifier combine many blocks' authenticators into one short response, stated to shrink communication per challenge from linear to constant in the number of blocks checked, and gives the first proof-of-retrievability scheme with a formal security proof. The construction whose asymptotic communication-cost claim a repair-and-audit design should be checked against rather than the earlier sentinel scheme.

title: Provable Data Possession at Untrusted Stores
authors: Giuseppe Ateniese, Randal C. Burns, Reza Curtmola, Joseph Herring, Lea Kissner, Zachary N. J. Peterson, Dawn Song
venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Introduces provable data possession, a different guarantee than proof of retrievability: the provider proves possession of most of the file via homomorphic tags checked over a random block sample, without the file being reconstructible from the proof exchange, and without necessarily proving the client could reconstruct the whole file if some blocks were in fact lost. The paper whose weaker-guarantee-but-lower-cost tradeoff a proof-of-retrievability design should be checked against by name, since the two guarantees are frequently conflated.

title: Proofs of Space
authors: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust, Vladimir Kolmogorov, Krzysztof Pietrzak
why_needed: Defines proof of space: a prover commits disk space by computing a hard-to-invert function of that size once, then answers later challenges cheaply, proving continued possession of the space without repeating the expensive computation. The primitive underlying proof-of-spacetime schemes (used by Filecoin and Chia) for proving storage over an interval of time without a per-challenge full rescan of the stored data.

title: Tight Proofs of Space and Replication
authors: Ben Fisch
why_needed: Formal treatment of proof of replication: a provider proves it stores n independent physical replicas of the same data (not one copy referenced n times) by proving each replica took at least a stated sequential computation time to produce from the data, with a formally proved lower bound on the adversary's cheating probability as a function of replica count and per-replica encoding depth. The academic construction underlying Filecoin's deployed Proof-of-Replication, stated with a security proof the whitepaper (BENET-FILECOIN-17) does not itself provide.

title: IPFS - Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System
authors: Juan Benet
why_needed: Origin description of the content-addressing mechanism underlying the InterPlanetary File System: every object is named by the cryptographic hash of its bytes, linked into a Merkle directed acyclic graph so that any subtree can be verified without re-hashing the whole graph, retrieved from any peer holding it via a distributed hash table keyed by that same hash. States the mechanism a person can implement; measured deployment behavior is in TRAUTWEIN-SIGCOMM-22.

title: Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web
authors: Dennis Trautwein, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Moritz Schubotz, Bela Gipp, Yiannis Psaras
why_needed: Deployed measurement of the live IPFS network's content-lookup and retrieval performance and content-popularity distribution, run against the network's actual population rather than a simulation, and identifies which components of the design (Bitswap block exchange, the Kademlia distributed hash table) dominate observed latency. The measurement study a content-addressing design's latency claims must be checked against.

title: Tahoe: The Least-Authority Filesystem
authors: Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn, Brian Warner
venue: ACM Workshop on Storage Security and Survivability (StorageSS)
why_needed: Deployed system combining erasure coding for durability with per-file capability-based encryption keys derived from the file's own content hash, so that possessing a read capability to a file is both the decryption key and the means of locating it, with no separate access-control server. States the specific erasure-code parameters used in production (3-of-10 default) and the storage-overhead-versus-durability tradeoff that setting implies.

title: SoK: Decentralized Storage Network
authors: Chuanlei Li, Minghui Xu, Jiahao Zhang, Hechuan Guo, Xiuzhen Cheng
why_needed: 2024 systematization of knowledge across deployed decentralized storage networks (the brief's explicit ask for a post-2023 SoK in this area), classifying their storage-verification mechanisms (proof of replication, proof of spacetime, proof of storage), redundancy schemes, and incentive designs on a common set of axes. Use to check that no major deployed system or mechanism family is missing from this target list before closing out domain C.

title: Filecoin: A Decentralized Storage Network
authors: Juan Benet, Nicola Greco
why_needed: Describes the deployed pairing of Proof-of-Replication (a storage provider proves n independent physical copies of client data) and Proof-of-Spacetime (the provider repeats a cheap proof at intervals, so a provider that deletes the data fails the next one) as the verification layer behind a market matching clients wanting durability against providers offering disk space, with the specific sealing and window-post proof intervals used in production. The deployed system FISCH-EUROCRYPT-19 supplies the formal security treatment for.

title: Sia: Simple Decentralized Storage
authors: David Vorick, Luke Champine
why_needed: Describes a storage-contract design in which a client and a storage host jointly sign a smart-contract-style agreement specifying data, price, and a schedule of storage proofs, settled without a third-party escrow. A different incentive-and-verification structure than Filecoin's for the same underlying proof-of-storage problem, needed to compare the two mechanisms' cost and trust assumptions rather than treat Filecoin's design as the only deployed answer.

title: Storj: A Decentralized Cloud Storage Network Framework
authors: Shawn Wilkinson and Storj Labs, Inc.
why_needed: Describes a design that erasure-codes each file, distributes pieces to independent storage nodes under per-piece audit contracts, and states a target storage-overhead ratio for the deployed network. A third deployed erasure-coded storage design (alongside Filecoin's replication-based and Sia's contract-based approaches) whose stated overhead figure needs checking against what the network's own repair mechanism requires to sustain it, per the brief's ban on taking a single deployed system's parameter as the only possible value.

title: Arweave: A Protocol for Economically Sustainable Information Permanence
authors: Sam Williams, Viktor Diordiiev, Lev Berman, Ivan Uemlianin
why_needed: Describes a design that pays once for storage intended to persist indefinitely, using a proof-of-access consensus rule that requires each block producer to present a copy of a randomly selected past block before it can produce a new one, which is stated to reward replication of rarely accessed old data rather than only frequently requested recent data. A durability model structurally different from Filecoin's, Sia's, and Storj's per-contract renewal model, needed as a distinct point of comparison for the one-time-payment-for-permanence design question.

title: Walrus: An Efficient Decentralized Storage Network
authors: George Danezis, Giacomo Giuliari, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Markus Legner, Jean-Pierre Smith, Alberto Sonnino, Karl Wust
venue: arXiv preprint (2025); also published as a systems conference paper
why_needed: 2025 storage-network design using two-dimensional erasure coding (RedStuff) specifically to lower the per-piece repair bandwidth of prior single-dimension erasure-coded designs (Storj, Sia) while tolerating Byzantine (contradictory-message-sending) storage nodes, with a stated storage-overhead figure. Cited by the prior pass at overhead 3.5 against Storj's 1.75; both figures require verification against this paper's own full text before being carried into the evidence file, per the rule against citing prior-pass characterizations as measurements.

title: Set Reconciliation with Nearly Optimal Communication Complexity
authors: Yaron Minsky, Ari Trachtenberg, Richard Zippel
why_needed: Characteristic-polynomial set reconciliation: two peers exchange evaluations of a rational function whose roots are the set elements, recovering the symmetric difference in near-optimal bits but requiring the difference size to be known or bounded in advance. This is the predecessor line every range-based and rateless scheme in this domain compares against.

title: Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables
authors: Michael T. Goodrich, Michael Mitzenmacher
venue: 49th Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing
why_needed: Introduces the Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT), a hash-table variant supporting a peeling decode that recovers listed keys from a fixed-size summary; the data structure every Difference-Digest-family set-reconciliation scheme in this domain builds on.

title: What's the Difference? Efficient Set Reconciliation Without Prior Context
authors: David Eppstein, Michael T. Goodrich, Frank Uyeda, George Varghese
why_needed: Difference Digests: an IBLT-based protocol that reconciles two sets in communication proportional to the symmetric-difference size without either side knowing that size beforehand, using invertible Bloom filters sized by an estimator. This is the deployed-scale foundation of the IBLT reconciliation family, and its per-hop bandwidth figures are the numbers a range-based scheme's claimed advantage must be checked against.

title: Practical Rateless Set Reconciliation
authors: Lei Yang, Yossi Gilad, Mohammad Alizadeh
why_needed: Rateless IBLT: an encoder that produces an unbounded stream of coded symbols from the set difference so the decoder stops as soon as it has received enough, removing the need to size the sketch in advance at all. States its own measured range of tested set-difference sizes and payload sizes; this is the foundational paper of the rateless-coded reconciliation family named in this domain's brief.

title: CertainSync: Rateless Set Reconciliation with Certainty
authors: Tomer Keniagin, Eitan Yaakobi, Ori Rottenstreich
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Measurement and Analysis of Computing Systems (SIGMETRICS)
why_needed: Addresses the failure condition rateless IBLT leaves open: decode can fail to terminate or return a wrong result with some probability. Extract what guarantee of successful termination this construction proves and at what overhead relative to Yang et al., since a synchronization primitive without a termination bound has an open failure mode the architecture must account for.

title: Rateless Bloom Filters: Set Reconciliation for Divergent Replicas with Variable-Sized Elements
authors: Pedro Silva Gomes, Carlos Baquero
why_needed: Applies rateless coding to reconciliation of variable-length elements rather than fixed-length hashes, authored by one of the original CRDT co-authors (Baquero). Elements in a replicated log or CRDT operation history are variable-length, so this states whether rateless reconciliation composes with that data shape without a length-normalization step.

title: Range-Based Set Reconciliation via Range-Summarizable Order-Statistics Stores
authors: Elvio G. Amparore
why_needed: Formalizes the storage-backend contract range-based set reconciliation (RBSR) needs (composable range summaries plus rank/select navigation), separates protocol complexity from storage complexity, augments B+-trees to realize it, and implements it as AELMDB integrated with Negentropy. Directly answers this domain's brief to find 2023-2026 work separating RBSR's protocol complexity from its local computational cost, and gives measured local-reconciliation-cost results on reconciliation-heavy workloads.

title: Range-Based Set Reconciliation Without Homomorphic Hashing
authors: Aljoscha Meyer, Konstantin Scherer
venue: Technical report, Technische Universität Berlin (self-published, author's site)
why_needed: Replaces range-based set reconciliation's requirement for a non-standard homomorphic hash function with an implementation over history-independent, clamping-invariant search trees usable with any conventional hash (e.g. SHA-family), removing a cryptographic-primitive dependency the 2023 SRDS paper had. Also directly compares against Merkle Search Trees (Auvolat and Taïani) on the same complexity criteria; extract that comparison's measured or derived basis rather than the paper's own 'renders MST reconciliation obsolete' claim, which is the authors' judgment, not a fact to carry forward per this pass's rule 2.

title: Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks
authors: Alex Auvolat, François Taïani
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Reliable Distributed Systems (SRDS)
why_needed: Merkle Search Tree (MST): a probabilistic balanced search tree whose node boundaries and structure are determined only by the content (history-independent), so that two replicas holding the same key set converge to an identical tree regardless of insertion order, letting the tree itself serve as a state-based CRDT and support Merkle-style content comparison for reconciliation. States the paper Meyer and Scherer (2024) directly compare against and claim to obsolete; both comparisons need this primary source's own numbers.

title: Accelerating Prolly Trees: Simplified Chunking for Rapid Updates
authors: Abhimanyu Rawat, Tarun Kumar Vangani, Hanno Cornelius, Vanesa Daza
why_needed: Prolly trees are content-defined-chunked B-trees where every node is content-addressed, giving Merkle-tree-style verification plus B-tree-style ordered range scans. States a deterministic chunking algorithm bounding a single insertion's restructuring to one chunk plus an O(height) anchor-path update, replacing the classical design's cascading rechunking, with measured hash-operation counts and insertion-time reductions on real workloads. Directly answers the brief's open question on 2023-2026 work on secondary indexes and range queries over content-addressed stores. An extended journal version appears in ACM Distributed Ledger Technologies: Research and Practice (DOI 10.1145/3785142).

title: Cartesian Merkle Tree
authors: Artem Chystiakov, Oleh Komendant, Kyrylo Riabov
why_needed: Combines a binary search tree, a heap (treap structure), and a Merkle tree into one history-independent structure supporting O(log n) insertion, update, and removal plus membership and non-membership proofs. A treap-family alternative to Merkle Search Trees and to Meyer's zip-tree-based constructions for the same history-independence property RBSR over search trees requires; needed to compare tree-balancing mechanisms (randomized priority vs. content-derived split points) for the same convergence guarantee.

title: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types
authors: Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski
venue: Stabilization, Safety, and Security of Distributed Systems (SSS)
why_needed: States the two sufficient conditions for strong eventual consistency without coordination: state-based (CvRDT) replicas whose merge is a join on a semilattice, and operation-based (CmRDT) replicas whose concurrent operations commute, each proved sufficient in this paper. Every later CRDT paper in this domain is built on one of these two conditions, so a mechanism's classification as CvRDT or CmRDT determines what convergence proof it can reuse.

title: Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types
authors: Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski
venue: Bulletin of the European Association for Theoretical Computer Science (EATCS), No. 104
why_needed: Expository classification of the CvRDT/CmRDT families with worked examples (counters, sets, sequences) at more length than the SSS conference paper; the open-access companion piece to cite for the taxonomy itself rather than for the formal proofs.

title: Approaches to Conflict-free Replicated Data Types
authors: Paulo Sérgio Almeida
why_needed: 2025 systematization of CRDT design approaches (operation-based, state-based, pure operation-based, delta-state) by one of the delta-state CRDT co-inventors. This is the domain's post-2023 survey and the source to check for which CRDT design questions the field considers open versus settled as of 2025, ahead of any per-mechanism selection.

title: Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality
authors: Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Hongseok Yang, Marek Zawirski
venue: ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL)
why_needed: Gives a formal, executable specification framework for replicated data types independent of any implementation, plus a proof technique for showing a given implementation meets a specification and a notion of optimality (no implementation can send less information and still meet the spec). Needed as the formal-methods yardstick for any measured-cost claim about a specific CRDT implementation in this domain.

title: A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford
venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
why_needed: The algorithm underlying Automerge: a CRDT for arbitrary nested JSON (maps, lists, and ordered text) built from a list CRDT with each list element addressed by a globally unique, causally-ordered identifier. States the paper's own memory and message-size measurements against Operational Transformation and other CRDTs, which is the primary source for any claim about Automerge's baseline cost before later encoding optimizations.

title: OpSets: Sequential Specifications for Replicated Datatypes
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Victor B. F. Gomes, Dominic P. Mulligan, Alastair R. Beresford
why_needed: Machine-checked (Isabelle/HOL) formal framework proving that a family of list, map, and JSON CRDTs satisfy list/map sequential-specification semantics, independent of network delivery order. Needed as the machine-verified correctness backing for the JSON CRDT and text-editing CRDTs selected elsewhere in this domain; an extended version with the informal exposition is arXiv:1805.04263.

title: Interleaving Anomalies in Collaborative Text Editors
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Victor B. F. Gomes, Dominic P. Mulligan, Alastair R. Beresford
venue: Workshop on Principles and Practice of Consistency for Distributed Data (PaPoC), co-located with EuroSys
why_needed: States a correctness failure common to RGA-family sequence CRDTs (the family underlying much of Yjs and early Automerge): when two users concurrently insert text at the same position, some of these algorithms can interleave the two users' characters into a garbled result rather than keeping each contiguous. Extract the precise condition under which interleaving occurs and which named algorithms are and are not subject to it, since this bears directly on which sequence-CRDT variant is safe to select for collaborative text.

title: Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing
authors: Hagit Attiya, Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Adam Morrison, Hongseok Yang, Marek Zawirski
venue: ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC)
why_needed: Gives a formal correctness specification for collaborative text editing and proves a worst-case lower bound on the memory any correct algorithm must retain (a function of the number of concurrent edits), independent of which specific CRDT or OT algorithm is used. This is the primary source for a memory-cost floor to check any measured CRDT text-editing footprint in this domain against. An extended journal version with a tightened space bound is Theoretical Computer Science 855 (2021), DOI 10.1016/j.tcs.2020.11.046.

title: A Highly-Available Move Operation for Replicated Trees
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Dominic P. Mulligan, Victor B. F. Gomes, Alastair R. Beresford
venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
why_needed: A CRDT for a mutable tree (the data model of a filesystem directory hierarchy or a nested outline) supporting a move operation that concurrent operations from other replicas cannot turn into a cycle, without coordination. Needed wherever the application data model is a hierarchical structure rather than a flat map or sequence, which the flat JSON CRDT of Kleppmann and Beresford (2017) does not by itself resolve for move semantics.

title: Yjs: A Framework for Near Real-Time P2P Shared Editing on Arbitrary Data Types
authors: Petru Nicolaescu, Kevin Jahns, Michael Derntl, Ralf Klamma
why_needed: The original paper describing Yjs's shared-editing framework and its internal replicated data-type representation, needed as the primary source for how Yjs's mechanism differs internally from Automerge's JSON CRDT even though both target the same class of collaborative-editing problem; a follow-up, 'Near Real-Time Peer-to-Peer Shared Editing on Extensible Data Types' (GROUP 2016), extends the same system.

title: Making CRDTs Byzantine Fault Tolerant
authors: Martin Kleppmann
venue: Workshop on Principles and Practice of Consistency for Distributed Data (PaPoC), co-located with EuroSys
why_needed: Extends the state-based and operation-based CRDT convergence proofs to a Byzantine setting, where some replicas may send different, contradictory operations to different recipients, using hash-chained operation logs so any two correct replicas that received the same log entries compute the same state even if a faulty replica tried to make them diverge. States the mechanism BeeKEM (already retrieved) explicitly builds on and cites as its CRDT foundation.

title: Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Heidi Howard
why_needed: Defines Byzantine Eventual Consistency (BEC) as a correctness condition for peer-to-peer databases with malicious participants, and proves an impossibility result bounding what such a system can guarantee without a trusted party. Needed as the source for what causal-broadcast and CRDT convergence can and cannot promise once some peers are actively malicious rather than merely crash-faulty, ahead of the Byzantine-CRDT mechanism above.

title: Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems
authors: Clarence A. Ellis, Simon J. Gibbs
why_needed: The original Operational Transformation (OT) paper: concurrent operations are transformed against each other so that, applied in a different order at each site, they still produce the same final document, requiring a central sequencer or agreed total order in the algorithms this paper presents. Needed as the OT baseline this domain's brief asks for, to compare against the CRDT family's ordering requirements.

title: Operational Transformation in Real-Time Group Editors: Issues, Algorithms, and Achievements
authors: Chengzheng Sun, Clarence A. Ellis
venue: ACM Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW)
why_needed: States the transformation-property requirements (TP1, TP2) later OT algorithms must satisfy to remain correct under arbitrary concurrent-operation orderings, and surveys where early OT algorithms violated them. Needed as the source for OT's own stated correctness conditions and failure modes, for a fair comparison against CRDT convergence guarantees rather than an comparison against an unstated or idealized version of OT.

title: High-Latency, Low-Bandwidth Windowing in the Jupiter Collaboration System
authors: David A. Nichols, Pavel Curtis, Michael Dixon, John Lamping
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
why_needed: The Jupiter protocol: a client-server OT scheme in which the server imposes total order and each client transforms its own pending operations against the server's acknowledged operation stream. This client-server OT design (later the basis of Google Wave's and Google Docs's OT implementations) is the direct point of comparison for why decentralized CRDT and Byzantine causal broadcast approaches in this domain avoid requiring a server to impose order.

title: Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in Spite of the Cloud
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg, Mark McGranaghan
venue: ACM SIGPLAN International Symposium on New Ideas, New Paradigms, and Reflections on Programming and Software (Onward!)
why_needed: States seven requirements for local-first software (no spinners: work is fast; multi-device; offline-capable; supports real-time collaboration; the long now, meaning data readable indefinitely; privacy and security by default; user retains ultimate ownership and control) and argues CRDTs are the mechanism that satisfies several of them simultaneously. This is the requirements document the CRDT and synchronization mechanisms in this domain are being selected to satisfy, not itself a mechanism paper.

title: ListGuard: Mitigating Pollution Attacks on In-Network Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables
authors: Harish S A, Vignesh S, Sathwik Kodamarthi, Bikraj Shrestha, Gollapudi Sasank, Mahanth Kumar Valluri, Pravein G. Kannan, Praveen Tammana
why_needed: A pollution attack against in-network IBLT-based reconciliation: extract the injection mechanism that corrupts peeling decode and the measured decode-failure or false-recovery rate it causes, and the defense (ListGuard) proposed against it, since this bears directly on whether IBLT-based reconciliation is safe against an adversarial peer without added integrity checks.

title: Breaking 2-Cores for Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables by Structure Prediction
authors: Vojtech Gadurek, Pavel Veselý
