why_needed: Attacks the peeling-decode guarantee of IBLTs by predicting and exploiting 2-core structure (the substructure that makes standard peeling decode fail), open access via LIPIcs. Extract the measured decode-failure rate this construction forces at set sizes and load factors otherwise considered safe for IBLT decode, which bears on the safety margin any IBLT-based reconciliation parameter choice needs against an adversarial peer.

title: Willow: 3d Range-Based Set Reconciliation (protocol specification)
authors: Sam Gwilym, Aljoscha Meyer, and the Earthstar/Willow project contributors
venue: willowprotocol.org, protocol specification (not a peer-reviewed paper), funded in part by NLnet
why_needed: Generalizes range-based set reconciliation from a single ordered dimension to a 3-dimensional range (subspace, path, timestamp), so one reconciliation round can target the intersection of a namespace, a path prefix, and a time window instead of the whole ordered set. This is the deployed generalization named directly in this domain's brief; extract its concrete fingerprint-composition rule and how it partitions a 3dRange to recurse, since this is the working answer to whether range-based reconciliation extends to structured, multi-dimensional data rather than one flat ordered log.

title: NIP-77: Negentropy Syncing (Nostr protocol extension for range-based set reconciliation)
authors: Doug Hoyte (Negentropy protocol), wrapped for Nostr as NIP-77 by the nostr-protocol contributors
venue: github.com/nostr-protocol/nips and github.com/hoytech/negentropy, protocol specification (not a peer-reviewed paper)
why_needed: The deployed range-based-reconciliation implementation this domain's brief names directly, and the integration target of Amparore (2026)'s AELMDB storage backend. Its wire format fixes concrete parameters (fingerprint = SHA-256 of the modular sum of element IDs concatenated with the element count, truncated to 16 bytes; a Bound encodes a timestamp plus a variable-length disambiguating ID prefix) that give one real answer to how a homomorphic-style fingerprint is built from a conventional hash by using modular addition as the combining operation, relevant to Meyer and Scherer's homomorphic-hashing objection.

title: Escaping the Evils of Centralized Control with Self-certifying Pathnames
authors: David Mazières, M. Frans Kaashoek
why_needed: Defines the self-certifying name construction (name = hash of the holder's public key, holder signs the binding to current content/state) that every later self-certifying-identity and self-certifying-content-address scheme reuses; the formal precursor to IPNS-style naming this repo's evidence file needs before evaluating any naming-ledger alternative.

title: Names: Decentralized, Secure, Human-Meaningful: Choose Two (the original statement of Zooko's triangle)
authors: Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn
why_needed: Original formulation of the three-property naming trilemma (decentralized, secure, human-meaningful — pick two) that every naming-ledger, self-certifying-name, and 'escapes Zooko's triangle' claim in this domain must be checked against; not a peer-reviewed paper, so any measured claim from it must stay labeled accordingly.

title: CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users
authors: Marcela S. Melara, Aaron Blankstein, Joseph Bonneau, Edward W. Felten, Michael J. Freedman
why_needed: Foundational key-transparency design: a verifiable Merkle-tree directory of name-to-key bindings, signed and chained epoch-to-epoch, letting a user detect a substituted key by monitoring only their own entry. Every later key-transparency system (SEEMless, Merkle^2, Parakeet) states its own contribution as an improvement against this baseline, so its cost figures (proof size, update latency) are the comparison point.

title: SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less</> Trust
authors: Melissa Chase, Apoorvaa Deshpande, Esha Ghosh, Harjasleen Malvai
why_needed: States a key-transparency directory built for update throughput at messaging-provider scale (verifiable random functions for hidden lookups, batched Merkle updates), positioned directly against CONIKS's design; needed for the throughput-versus-privacy comparison among key-transparency candidates.

title: Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
authors: Harjasleen Malvai, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino, Esha Ghosh, Ercan Öztürk, Kevin Lewi, Sean F. Lawlor
why_needed: Written by the WhatsApp/Meta key-transparency team; extends CONIKS/SEEMless with bounded-size compaction and threshold-witness signing at billions-of-updates-per-week scale, and is the paper the deployed WhatsApp Auditable Key Directory (announced by Meta engineering, April 2023, publicly audited by Cloudflare from 2023) implements. Needed as the deployed-scale evidence point for the key-transparency component decision.

title: Merkle^2: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System
authors: Yuncong Hu, Kian Hooshmand, Harika Kalidhindi, Seung Jin Yang, Raluca Ada Popa
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
why_needed: A two-dimensional Merkle-tree construction (one dimension over identities, one over time) aimed at reducing key-transparency proof latency; the specific alternative to CONIKS/Parakeet's single-tree-per-epoch design and the source for whichever latency figures decide between them.

title: An Empirical Study of Namecoin and Lessons for Decentralized Namespace Design
authors: Harry A. Kalodner, Miles Carlsten, Paul Ellenbogen, Joseph Bonneau, Arvind Narayanan
venue: Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS)
why_needed: Independent measurement of a deployed blockchain naming ledger: how many names were actually registered, squatted, or left unused, and what that implies for consensus-secured human-readable naming as an approach to the Zooko's-triangle third property. Needed as the deployment-scale counterpoint to any theoretical naming-ledger proposal.

title: A Censorship-Resistant, Privacy-Enhancing and Fully Decentralized Name System
authors: Matthias Wachs, Martin Schanzenbach, Christian Grothoff
venue: International Conference on Cryptology and Network Security (CANS)
why_needed: Defines the GNU Name System: per-user private name-to-key mappings with no global consensus and no global uniqueness, the structural opposite of Namecoin/ENS/Handshake's ledger-consensus approach to the same trilemma corner. Needed to state the consensus-free naming alternative's cost (each user resolves a different meaning for the same name) as fact rather than by assumption.

title: Challenges in Decentralized Name Management: The Case of ENS
authors: Pengcheng Xia, Haoyu Wang, Zhou Yu, Xinyu Liu, Xiapu Luo, Guoai Xu, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: First large-scale measurement of the Ethereum Name Service naming ledger, reporting security problems specific to a blockchain-consensus naming design (not present in classic DNS) alongside legacy DNS-style problems it inherits. Needed as the empirical test of whether a ledger-based naming system that claims to give a readable, secure, decentralized name actually delivers all three at deployment scale, rather than only in the design document.

title: Handshake: A Decentralized, Permissionless Naming Protocol Compatible with the Domain Name System
authors: Handshake project (collective; whitepaper unattributed to named individuals in the retrieved copy)
why_needed: Describes a proof-of-work blockchain used only to secure the DNS root zone (top-level names), leaving lower DNS levels to existing infrastructure — a narrower-scope alternative to Namecoin/ENS's whole-namespace ledger. Not a peer-reviewed source; any number from it enters the evidence file only as project-stated design intent, not as a measured fact, per the citing-abstracts rule extended to project documents.

title: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0
authors: W3C Credentials Community Group / DID Working Group (Manu Sporny, Amy Guy, Markus Sabadello, Drummond Reed, editors)
why_needed: The normative specification of the DID URI scheme and its resolution/verification data model, which every decentralized-identifier implementation (including the DID methods used by verifiable-credential and self-sovereign-identity systems in this domain) must conform to for interoperability. Needed as the primary definitional source rather than a secondary description of DIDs.

title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
authors: W3C Verifiable Credentials Working Group (Manu Sporny, Ted Thibodeau Jr., Ivan Herman, Michael B. Jones, Gabe Cohen, editors)
why_needed: The normative data model for verifiable credentials (issuer, subject, claims, proof) that BBS+-based and other anonymous-credential schemes in this domain implement as a concrete credential format. Needed as the primary definitional source before evaluating any anonymous-credential proof system built to issue or present credentials in this format.

title: Secure Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Based Cryptosystems
authors: Rosario Gennaro, Stanislaw Jarecki, Hugo Krawczyk, Tal Rabin
why_needed: Identifies a flaw in the earlier Pedersen distributed-key-generation protocol (a rushing adversary can bias the output key) and gives the corrected construction, making this the correctness-baseline DKG protocol that every threshold-signature or threshold-decryption scheme for group identity keys must be checked against. Needed before selecting any DKG for a guardian-quorum key-recovery or threshold-signing identity component.

title: Non-Interactive and Information-Theoretic Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing
authors: Torben P. Pedersen
why_needed: Gives the verifiable secret-sharing scheme (participants can check their share is consistent with a public commitment, without revealing the secret) that distributed key generation and guardian-quorum social recovery both build on. Needed as the mechanism a later synthesis cites when a key-recovery or threshold-key-generation component claims share verifiability.

title: How to Share a Secret
authors: Adi Shamir
why_needed: Defines (k,n)-threshold secret sharing via polynomial interpolation over a finite field: any k of n shares reconstruct the secret, fewer than k reveal nothing information-theoretically. This is the arithmetic every guardian-quorum key-recovery scheme in this domain (and every threshold-signature DKG) reduces to; needed as the primitive-level citation beneath both.

title: FROST: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures
authors: Chelsea Komlo, Ian Goldberg
why_needed: A threshold Schnorr signature scheme requiring only one round of signer communication in the common case (versus prior threshold-Schnorr protocols' multiple rounds), with a security proof against Boneh-Drijvers-Neven-style rogue-key attacks; the round-count figure and the security model it targets are the numbers a later synthesis needs when comparing threshold-signing latency against BLS threshold signatures. Standardized afterward as IETF RFC 9591 (2024), which is the deployment-adoption signal for this specific scheme over its predecessors.

title: Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing
authors: Dan Boneh, Ben Lynn, Hovav Shacham
why_needed: Introduces the BLS signature scheme: a pairing-based signature shorter than DSA/Schnorr at equivalent security, and the only common signature scheme whose signatures on different messages by different keys can be combined into one constant-size aggregate that a verifier checks against the list of (message, public key) pairs. This aggregation property is the reason every threshold- and multi-signature scheme in this domain (Boldyreva, BDN, FROST as contrast) is built on or compared against BLS.

title: Threshold Signatures, Multisignatures and Blind Signatures Based on the Gap-Diffie-Hellman-Group Signature Scheme
authors: Alexandra Boldyreva
why_needed: Gives the threshold and multi-signature variants of BLS with a formal security proof, so any (k,n)-threshold BLS identity-key scheme in this domain traces its unforgeability guarantee to this paper rather than to an informal extension of the base BLS scheme.

title: Aggregate and Verifiably Encrypted Signatures from Bilinear Maps
authors: Dan Boneh, Craig Gentry, Ben Lynn, Hovav Shacham
why_needed: Gives the aggregate-signature construction proper (n signatures on n distinct messages from n distinct keys compressed to one signature of the same size as a single BLS signature), distinct from the threshold case in Boldyreva 2003 (n signers on one message). Needed because a group-membership or governance-quorum identity feature that batches many different signers' distinct attestations into one verification cost depends on this construction, not on threshold BLS.

title: Simple Schnorr Multi-Signatures with Applications to Bitcoin
authors: Gregory Maxwell, Andrew Poelstra, Yannick Seurin, Pieter Wuille
why_needed: MuSig: an interactive (multi-round) Schnorr multi-signature scheme with a rogue-key-attack proof, on ordinary elliptic-curve groups with no pairing requirement — the non-pairing alternative to BLS aggregation for combining several identity keys' signatures into one. Needed as the pairing-versus-no-pairing tradeoff evidence (round count added versus pairing-library dependency removed) for the multi-signature component decision.

title: Compact Multi-Signatures for Smaller Blockchains
authors: Dan Boneh, Manu Drijvers, Gregory Neven
why_needed: Gives a pairing-based multi-signature ("BDN") that removes the interactive key-aggregation-commitment round earlier BLS-based multi-signature schemes needed to block rogue-key attacks, at the cost of a proof-of-possession requirement per key at registration time. Needed as the specific improvement-over-earlier-BLS-multisig figure (round count removed, one-time proof-of-possession added) that a synthesis decision between MuSig, plain threshold BLS, and this scheme must cite.

title: Short Group Signatures
authors: Dan Boneh, Xavier Boyen, Hovav Shacham
why_needed: Introduces the BBS group signature scheme (a member proves membership in a group and signs a message without revealing which member, under a group manager who can revoke anonymity), the direct algebraic predecessor of the BBS+ signature scheme used for anonymous and zero-knowledge credentials. Needed before evaluating any BBS+-based verifiable-credential proposal, because BBS+'s change from this scheme (dropping the group-manager de-anonymization capability, adding multi-message signing) is the entire point of the later construction.

title: Anonymous Attestation Using the Strong Diffie-Hellman Assumption Revisited
authors: Jan Camenisch, Manu Drijvers, Anja Lehmann
venue: International Conference on Trust and Trustworthy Computing (TRUST)
why_needed: The paper that formalizes and proves security for what the field now calls BBS+: a signature scheme on a vector of messages, from which the holder proves knowledge of a signature and selectively discloses a subset of the signed messages in zero knowledge, with a formal unforgeability and anonymity proof the original informal 'BBS+' folklore construction lacked. This is the citation a verifiable-credential or selective-disclosure identity component needs before adopting BBS+ as its signature primitive.

title: SoK: Anonymous Credentials
authors: Saqib A. Kakvi, Keith M. Martin, Colin Putman, Elizabeth A. Quaglia
why_needed: Systematization of Knowledge unifying the anonymous-credential literature (CL signatures, BBS+, U-Prove, idemix and their selective-disclosure and unlinkability properties) under one comparison framework. Needed as the entry point for choosing among anonymous-credential constructions with a stated, citable basis for the comparison rather than an ad hoc one.

title: SoK: Anonymous Credentials for Digital Identity Wallets
authors: Christian Bormann, Anja Lehmann
venue: Security Standardisation Research (SSR); extended version IACR ePrint 2026
why_needed: A 2025 follow-up SoK specifically scoped to the credential schemes under active standardization for government and EU digital-identity wallets (which constrains the anonymous-credential design space differently than the 2023 general SoK). Needed to check whether the credential scheme selected for this architecture's identity layer matches or diverges from what deployed-wallet standardization is converging on, and why.

title: A Survey on Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials
authors: Carlo Mazzocca, Abbas Acar, A. Selcuk Uluagac, Rebecca Montanari, Paolo Bellavista, Mauro Conti
venue: IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials (arXiv preprint 2024, journal version 2025)
why_needed: Surveys the DID/verifiable-credential ecosystem (methods, resolution infrastructure, wallet architectures, trust models) as a whole rather than the credential cryptography alone. Needed as the systems-level complement to the Kakvi/Bormann cryptographic SoKs when this domain's evidence file states what a DID-based identity layer requires from the rest of the architecture (resolver availability, revocation infrastructure).

title: SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities
authors: Sushanth Ambati, Kainat Adeel, Jack Myers, Nikolay Ivanov
venue: ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies (SACMAT)
why_needed: The most recent (2026) Systematization of Knowledge on self-sovereign identity broadly, covering key management, recovery, and access-control aspects the two credential-focused SoKs above do not center. Needed to catch any 2025-2026 result on identity-key recovery or governance that supersedes what the earlier SoKs recorded, per the brief's explicit requirement to check for work superseding older results.

title: Smart Contract-Based Social Recovery Wallet Management Scheme for Digital Assets
authors: Konstantin Pedin, Mais Nijim, Mohammadamin Sameni
why_needed: Gives a specific guardian-quorum key-recovery construction implemented as a smart contract (protected address, backup address, timelock, guardian threshold), one concrete point in the social-recovery design space this domain must evaluate against a non-blockchain-anchored recovery scheme built directly on Shamir/Pedersen secret sharing.

title: Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies
authors: Maria Borge, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Philipp Jovanovic, Linus Gasser, Nicolas Gailly, Bryan Ford
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (EuroS&PW)
why_needed: Defines the pseudonym-party construction for proof of personhood: participants convene in person at an announced time and place and each receives exactly one anonymous token, with no participant identified. This is the foundational non-biometric, non-social-graph proof-of-personhood mechanism every later scheme (BrightID's social-graph substitute, Idena's synchronous-puzzle substitute, Worldcoin's biometric substitute) replaces one part of, so needed as the baseline every substitution is a deviation from.

title: Who Watches the Watchmen? A Review of Subjective Approaches for Sybil-Resistance in Proof of Personhood Protocols
authors: Divya Siddarth, Sergey Ivliev, Santiago Siri, Paula Berman
why_needed: Critiques the social-graph and social-vouching family of proof-of-personhood schemes (the family BrightID and Proof of Humanity belong to) for depending on subjective human judgment calls at some point in the protocol, and analyzes the resulting exposure. Needed to extract the specific failure conditions of subjective-judgment-based proof of personhood as fact, separate from the paper's own framing of which tradeoffs are acceptable.

title: Personhood Credentials: Artificial Intelligence and the Value of Privacy-Preserving Tools to Distinguish Who Is Real Online
authors: Steven Adler, Zoë Hitzig, Shrey Jain, and 28 additional co-authors spanning OpenAI, Microsoft, MIT, and multiple civil-society and standards organizations
why_needed: Cross-institutional framework paper defining 'personhood credential' as a general category (a credential attesting uniqueness and humanness without necessarily identifying which human) and setting out the design requirements the category must meet (unlinkability across issuances, revocability, no single-issuer capture). Needed as the framework this domain's specific proof-of-personhood systems (Worldcoin, BrightID, Idena, Proof of Humanity) are instances of, so their designs can be checked against a stated requirement set rather than against each other only.

title: Personhood Credentials: Human-Centered Design Recommendation Balancing Security, Usability, and Trust
authors: Ayae Ide, Tanusree Sharma
why_needed: Systematically compares deployed proof-of-personhood systems (BrightID, Proof of Humanity, Gitcoin Passport, Idena among them named in the abstract) on usability and trust dimensions instead of cryptographic ones alone. Needed as the independent, cross-system comparison point rather than relying on each project's own claims about its own usability.

title: BrightID Whitepaper
authors: BrightID project (collective; not peer-reviewed)
why_needed: Primary source for the BrightID mechanism itself: a social connection graph seeded by a small trusted-seed set, scored by a GroupSybilRank-style algorithm run over the graph. Needed because the Siddarth et al. and Ide/Sharma papers critique and compare BrightID but do not themselves fully specify its mechanism; any mechanism claim must come from this primary source, and any number from it is project-stated, not measured.

title: Idena: Proof-of-Person Blockchain Technology Overview
authors: Idena project (collective; not peer-reviewed)
why_needed: Primary source for Idena's synchronous-ceremony proof of personhood: all candidates worldwide solve human-generated visual-reasoning puzzles ('flips') within one fixed global time window, so no single participant can complete two sessions. Needed as the mechanism description for the time-synchronization-based alternative to BrightID's social-graph and Worldcoin's biometric approaches; project-stated, not independently measured.

title: World (Worldcoin) Whitepaper
authors: Tools for Humanity (collective; not peer-reviewed)
why_needed: Primary source for the biometric-iris proof-of-personhood mechanism (local iris-hash computation on a purpose-built device, zero-knowledge-proof-gated World ID issuance) that the personhood-credential framework papers and the Ide/Sharma comparison reference but do not themselves fully specify. Any exposure claim (device-manufacturer trust, hardware supply-chain requirement) must be traced to this primary source and kept labeled as project-stated design intent rather than an independently measured property.

title: SPHINCS: Practical Stateless Hash-Based Signatures
authors: Daniel J. Bernstein, Daira Hopwood, Andreas Hülsing, Tanja Lange, Ruben Niederhagen, Louiza Papachristodoulou, Michael Schneider, Peter Schwabe, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn
why_needed: First practical hash-based signature scheme requiring no signer-side state to track across signatures (a stateful hash-based scheme that reuses a one-time key pair breaks security, which rules out stateful schemes for a long-lived identity key with no reliable state-persistence guarantee across devices). Needed as the foundational construction before evaluating its 2019 successor for post-quantum identity-key signing.

title: The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework
authors: Andreas Hülsing, Denis Butin, Stefan-Lukas Gazdag, Joost Rijneveld, Aziz Mohaisen (framework paper; NIST submission led by Bernstein, Hülsing, and additional co-authors)
why_needed: The improved, smaller-signature stateless hash-based scheme that became the basis for NIST's standardized post-quantum signature FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). Needed as the specific post-quantum signature candidate for a long-lived identity key that requires no stored per-signature state and rests only on hash-function security (no lattice or pairing assumption), the most conservative security assumption among the post-quantum options in this domain.

title: CRYSTALS-Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme
authors: Léo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrède Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehlé
venue: IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (TCHES)
why_needed: A lattice-based (module-LWE/module-SIS) post-quantum signature scheme with smaller signatures and faster verification than SPHINCS+, at the cost of resting on a newer, less-studied hardness assumption and requiring the signer to track state-free but still larger keys; became the basis for NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA). Needed as the size/speed-versus-assumption-age tradeoff point against SPHINCS+ for the post-quantum identity-signature component decision.

title: The Sybil Attack
authors: John R. Douceur
why_needed: States the identity-forgery problem and proves that without a logically centralized identity-issuing authority, no distributed protocol can bound the number of identities one entity presents, except under resource-parity and coordination assumptions the paper states as unrealistic. Every other target in this domain is a proposed way around, or a measurement of the limits of, this result.

title: SybilGuard: Defending Against Sybil Attacks via Social Networks
authors: Haifeng Yu, Michael Kaminsky, Phillip B. Gibbons, Abraham Flaxman
why_needed: First social-graph Sybil defense: bounds accepted Sybil identities per attack edge by intersecting random routes, assuming the honest region of the graph is fast-mixing. Originates the whole random-walk/random-route social-graph defense family that SybilLimit, SybilRank, SybilInfer, Ostra, Bazaar, Canal, and Integro all descend from or are compared against.

title: SybilLimit: A Near-Optimal Social Network Defense against Sybil Attacks
authors: Haifeng Yu, Phillip B. Gibbons, Michael Kaminsky, Feng Xiao
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: States a tightened bound on accepted Sybil identities per attack edge relative to SybilGuard (O(log n) versus O(sqrt(n log n))) under the same fast-mixing assumption; the number every later social-graph defense states its own improvement against. The IEEE/ACM Trans. Netw. 2010 journal version (doi 10.1109/TNET.2009.2034047) is the extended text.

title: Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services
authors: Qiang Cao, Michael Sirivianos, Xiaowei Yang, Tiago Pregueiro
why_needed: SybilRank: ranks accounts by the landing probability of short random walks from a trusted seed set rather than by pairwise random-route intersection; deployed at Tuenti (a production social network), giving a rare production-deployment measurement to compare against the purely simulated defenses.

title: SybilInfer: Detecting Sybil Nodes using Social Networks
authors: George Danezis, Prateek Mittal
why_needed: Replaces the deterministic random-route intersection of SybilGuard/SybilLimit with Bayesian inference over the whole social graph, returning a probability that each node is a Sybil rather than a binary accept/reject; states its own false-positive/false-negative tradeoff curve to compare against the deterministic schemes.

title: SybilBelief: A Semi-Supervised Learning Approach for Structure-Based Sybil Detection
authors: Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Mario Frank, Prateek Mittal
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
why_needed: Applies loopy belief propagation to a graph seeded with a small labeled set of known-honest and known-Sybil nodes, generalizing SybilRank's single-class seed to two-class semi-supervised inference; states an accuracy comparison against SybilRank and SybilInfer on the same graphs.

title: SybilSCAR: Sybil Detection in Online Social Networks via Local Rule Based Propagation
authors: Binghui Wang, Le Zhang, Neil Zhenqiang Gong
why_needed: States a unified local-rule propagation framework that it claims subsumes SybilRank, SybilBelief, and SybilFuse as special cases and gives a formal linear-approximation convergence guarantee that the earlier structure-only methods lack; the convergence proof is the specific thing to extract.

title: SybilFuse: Combining Local Attributes with Global Structure to Perform Robust Sybil Detection
authors: Peng Gao, Binghui Wang, Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Sanjeev R. Kulkarni, Kurt Thomas, Prateek Mittal
venue: IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (CNS)
why_needed: Combines per-node local classifier scores (account attributes) with global graph-propagation scores as a weighted-edge input to SybilBelief-style propagation, on a Tuenti dataset with two attackers evading detection differently; states a robustness comparison under structure-only attacks that pure graph methods do not survive.

title: Ostra: Leveraging Trust to Thwart Unwanted Communication
authors: Alan Mislove, Ansley Post, Peter Druschel, P. Krishna Gummadi
why_needed: Applies the same attack-edge-limiting idea as SybilGuard to message-delivery credit rather than identity acceptance: a sender consumes and later refunds a link-capacity credit along the social-graph path to the recipient, bounding unwanted messages per attack edge without any global computation. A distinct application of the same underlying assumption, with its own deployment-scale measurement (a crawl of an online social network).

title: Bazaar: Strengthening User Reputations in Online Marketplaces
authors: Ansley Post, Vijit Shah, Alan Mislove
why_needed: Applies the Ostra link-credit mechanism to marketplace transaction reputation instead of message delivery, computing a per-transaction risk score from network flow along the trust graph; evaluated on a crawl of a real online marketplace with measured fraud outcomes, giving comparison numbers for flow-based reputation against pure rating-count schemes.

title: Canal: Scaling Social Network-Based Sybil Tolerance Schemes
authors: Bimal Viswanath, Mainack Mondal, P. Krishna Gummadi, Alan Mislove, Ansley Post
why_needed: States that the per-query graph traversal cost of SybilGuard-family and Ostra/Bazaar-family schemes prevents deployment on graphs at real social-network scale, and gives a landmark-routing precomputation that answers the same queries approximately at far lower cost; carries the specific accuracy-versus-cost tradeoff numbers for approximate social-graph defenses.

title: Íntegro: Leveraging Victim Prediction for Robust Fake Account Detection in OSNs
authors: Yazan Boshmaf, Dionysios Logothetis, Georgos Siganos, Jorge Lería, José Lorenzo, Matei Ripeanu, Konstantin Beznosov
why_needed: States that fake accounts preferentially befriend a predictable subset of honest users ("victims") and that down-weighting edges to predicted victims before running SybilRank-style propagation raises detection robustness against an adversary who forms attack edges strategically rather than at random, the specific adversary construction Viswanath (SIGCOMM 2010) and Alvisi (S&P 2013) showed defeats prior schemes. The Computer & Security 2016 journal version (doi 10.1016/j.cose.2016.05.005) is the extended text with a Tuenti production deployment.

title: Whanau: A Sybil-proof Distributed Hash Table
authors: Chris Lesniewski-Laas, M. Frans Kaashoek
why_needed: Builds routing tables directly from the social graph via random-walk sampling so that lookup correctness depends only on the count of attack edges, not on the count of Sybil identities, tolerating O(n/log n) attack edges with O(sqrt(n) log n) state per node and constant-round lookups; the one target system in this domain that is itself a DHT rather than a classifier layered on one, giving a direct alternative to Kademlia-family routing under adversarial identity creation.

title: A Sybil-proof One-hop DHT
authors: Chris Lesniewski-Laas
why_needed: Precursor construction to Whanau: routes lookups through a small set of social-graph-sampled introducers in a single hop rather than Whanau's multi-hop layered routing table; states the earlier, simpler version of the sampling argument Whanau's proof builds on.

title: An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses
authors: Bimal Viswanath, Ansley Post, P. Krishna Gummadi, Alan Mislove
why_needed: Shows by direct simulation on four real social-graph datasets that SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, and a simple community-detection baseline all in fact perform local community detection around the trusted seed, that a graph whose honest region is itself partitioned into distinct communities is therefore more vulnerable regardless of which of these four schemes is used, and that an adversary who chooses which honest nodes to attach to (rather than attaching uniformly at random) is measurably more effective — the specific finding every later social-graph defense (Canal, Integro, SybilFuse) must be checked against.

title: SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks
authors: Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Alessandro Epasto, Silvio Lattanzi, Alessandro Panconesi
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: Unifies SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilRank, SybilInfer, and GateKeeper under one local-community-detection framework, states that the choice of community-detection subroutine changes detection accuracy substantially even holding the surrounding scheme fixed, and states that a simple degree/feature classifier already matches graph-based methods against a random-attachment adversary while no published method as of 2013 was sufficient against a targeted-attachment adversary — the exact gap the brief's open problem 3 asks whether anything since has closed. The 2014 Internet Mathematics journal version (doi 10.1080/15427951.2013.865685, "Communities, Random Walks, and Social Sybil Defense") is the extended text.

title: Measuring the Mixing Time of Social Graphs
authors: Abedelaziz Mohaisen, Aaram Yun, Yongdae Kim
why_needed: Directly measures the mixing time of real social graphs (Facebook, LiveJournal, and others) rather than assuming it; every social-graph Sybil defense's stated bound holds only for a fast-mixing honest region, so this is the primary-source check on whether that precondition holds in deployed graphs. Cited by both Viswanath (SIGCOMM 2010) and Alvisi (S&P 2013) as the source of the mixing-time concern each critique raises.

title: Uncovering Social Network Sybils in the Wild
authors: Zhi Yang, Christo Wilson, Xiao Wang, Tingting Gao, Ben Y. Zhao, Yafei Dai
why_needed: Ground-truth measurement of Sybil accounts banned by a real deployed social network operator (Renren), giving observed attack-edge counts, attachment strategy, and behavioral signatures from an actual adversary population rather than a simulated one — the comparison point for every synthetic-attacker evaluation among the targets above. The 2014 ACM TKDD journal version (doi 10.1145/2556609) is the extended text.

title: SybilDefender: Defend Against Sybil Attacks in Large Social Networks
authors: Wei Wei, Fengyuan Xu, Chiu C. Tan, Qun Li
why_needed: Uses short random walks from a single suspect node (rather than from a trusted seed set) to decide whether that node is a Sybil, and separately clusters detected Sybils into communities to remove them in bulk; states its own scalability numbers (walk length, node count) as a specific alternative to SybilRank's global-ranking approach.

title: Sybil-Resilient Online Content Voting
authors: Dinh Nguyen Tran, Bonan Min, Jinyang Li, Lakshminarayanan Subramanian
why_needed: SumUp: bounds the count of votes an adversary's Sybils can cast on a piece of content by max-flow capacity along the social graph from voters to a trusted set of vote collectors, adaptively throttling links whose flow saturates; a max-flow-based construction contemporaneous with and structurally distinct from the SybilGuard random-route family, applied to a content-voting rather than identity-admission problem.

title: The Eigentrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks
authors: Sepandar D. Kamvar, Mario T. Schlosser, Hector Garcia-Molina
why_needed: Computes each participant's single global trust score as the principal left eigenvector of the matrix of normalized pairwise ratings, requiring a pre-trusted seed set to guarantee convergence; the foundational global-reputation construction every later peer-to-peer reputation system (PowerTrust, HonestPeer, EERP) states its comparison against, and the concrete case of the seed-set centralization problem the brief's domain description flags.

title: PowerTrust: A Robust and Scalable Reputation System for Trusted Peer-to-Peer Computing
authors: Runfang Zhou, Kai Hwang
venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
why_needed: Exploits a measured power-law distribution in peer feedback frequency to select the most-rated peers as distributed random-walk seeds instead of a fixed pre-trusted set, stating a specific convergence-speed and accuracy comparison against EigenTrust on the same simulated eBay-derived rating distribution.

title: PeerTrust: Supporting Reputation-Based Trust for Peer-to-Peer Electronic Communities
authors: Li Xiong, Ling Liu
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
why_needed: Computes trust from three measured components (feedback received, total transaction count, feedback-source credibility) plus two context-adaptive weights, rather than a single eigenvector score; states its own simulation results on a P2P transaction model comparing against EigenTrust and a no-trust baseline, giving the multi-factor alternative's specific cost and accuracy numbers.

title: Attack-Resistant Trust Metrics for Public Key Certification
authors: Raph Levien, Alexander Aiken
why_needed: Originates the max-flow formulation of trust propagation later refined into the Advogato metric: trust flows from a seed set through a certification graph and each edge carries a capacity bounding how much trust it passes, so a single adversary-controlled identity is bounded by the capacity of its incoming edges rather than by network size. Levien's 2009 book chapter "Attack-Resistant Trust Metrics" (doi 10.1007/978-1-84800-356-9_5) is the direct Advogato-specific description; this 1998 paper is where the max-flow construction and its bound are proved.

title: Propagation Models for Trust and Distrust in Social Networks
authors: Cai-Nicolas Ziegler, Georg Lausen
why_needed: Appleseed: computes local group trust by injecting energy at a source node and spreading it along outgoing trust edges by a tunable spreading-factor parameter, rather than by max-flow; states its own accuracy comparison against Advogato's max-flow metric on the same trust graph, giving the energy-spreading alternative's specific tradeoff against the flow-capacity bound.

title: The Beta Reputation System
authors: Roslan Ismail, Audun Jøsang
why_needed: Models the expected probability of a good outcome from one participant as (positive ratings + 1) / (positive + negative ratings + 2), a beta-distribution posterior updated in constant time per rating with no global computation; the elementary bilateral-rating building block that later multi-factor systems (PeerTrust) and marketplace systems (Bazaar) combine with a graph-level mechanism rather than using alone.

title: Combating Web Spam with TrustRank
authors: Zoltán Gyöngyi, Hector Garcia-Molina, Jan O. Pedersen
why_needed: Biased PageRank walk seeded from a small manually-verified trusted page set, propagating trust along hyperlinks with attenuation per hop; designed for web spam rather than peer reputation, later adapted to peer-to-peer settings, so it states a distinct trust-seeding mechanism (manual verification of a small seed) to compare against EigenTrust's and PowerTrust's automatic seed selection.

title: HonestPeer: An Enhanced EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Systems
authors: Heba A. Kurdi
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
why_needed: States a modification to EigenTrust that redistributes query load away from the fixed pre-trusted seed set (the concentration effect the brief's domain description flags), reporting simulation numbers against unmodified EigenTrust on the same peer population; the specific claim to check is whether the redistribution still requires a seed set or removes the dependency entirely.

title: EERP: An Enhanced EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in Peer-to-Peer Networks
authors: Alanoud Alhussain, Heba A. Kurdi
why_needed: A second, later modification to EigenTrust's seed-concentration problem by an overlapping author with HonestPeer; states its own comparison against both unmodified EigenTrust and HonestPeer, which is the specific number needed to determine whether either enhancement actually removes the seed-set dependency or only reduces its measured effect.

title: TrustGuard: Countering Vulnerabilities in Reputation Management for Decentralized Overlay Networks
authors: Mudhakar Srivatsa, Li Xiong, Ling Liu
why_needed: States and measures strategic-oscillation (a peer alternating good and bad behavior to stay above a reputation threshold) and collusion (peers rating each other falsely high) as concrete attacks on transaction-based reputation systems, with a specific decay-weighted and collusion-detection countermeasure and its measured effect on attacker gain; the primary source for the collusion and self-promotion attack categories the domain brief lists.

title: The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms
authors: Eric Friedman, Paul Resnick
why_needed: Formal game-theoretic proof that when a low-reputation identity can be costlessly discarded and replaced (whitewashing), every equilibrium must either penalize newcomers relative to established identities or accept a lower level of cooperation than a costly-identity system achieves; the primary source for the whitewashing attack category and the specific reason identity-creation cost enters the design at all.

title: A Survey of Attack and Defense Techniques for Reputation Systems
authors: Kevin Hoffman, David Zage, Cristina Nita-Rotaru
why_needed: Decomposes published reputation systems into a common set of components (rating, aggregation, storage, punishment) and classifies attacks by which component they target, giving a structured taxonomy of self-promotion, slandering, whitewashing, and identity-multiplication (Sybil) attacks against reputation specifically, each cited to its originating system; the single most exhaustive attack-classification source named in this domain.

title: Computational Puzzles as Sybil Defenses
authors: Nikita Borisov
venue: IEEE International Conference on Peer-to-Peer Computing (P2P)
why_needed: States the core difficulty in using proof-of-work against Sybil creation — a solved puzzle must not be reusable, or an attacker solves once and replays the solution for every identity — and gives a decentralized all-to-all challenge-broadcast construction whose combining function proves each solution incorporated a fresh challenge from every other participant; the foundational forgery-cost construction for the proof-of-work sub-family named in the domain brief.

title: Resource Burning for Permissionless Systems
authors: Diksha Gupta, Jared Saia, Maxwell Young
why_needed: Generalizes proof-of-work into "resource burning" — any mechanism that forces an entity to provably waste a scarce, unforgeable resource (computation, bandwidth, storage, or time) as the price of an identity or an action — and surveys the design space and known bounds across resource types, not only computation; states which resource choices admit provable Sybil-resistance bounds and which remain open, directly relevant to whether a non-computational resource can substitute for a trusted seed identity.

title: Interpreting Graph-Based Sybil Detection Methods as Low-Pass Filtering
authors: Satoshi Furutani, Toshiki Shibahara, Mitsuaki Akiyama, Masaki Aida
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
why_needed: Recasts SybilRank, SybilBelief, and related propagation-based detectors as instances of graph signal low-pass filtering, and uses that unification to state a shared structural limitation — the filtering view exposes exactly which graph-frequency components each method is blind to — providing a theoretical rather than empirical critique that applies across the whole propagation-based family at once, including the newer GNN-based detectors.

title: Enhancing Sybil Detection via Social-Activity Networks: A Random Walk Approach
authors: Xiaoying Zhang, Hong Xie, Pei Yi, John C. S. Lui
venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing
why_needed: Extends random-walk Sybil detection from the pure social graph to a joint social-activity network (edges from both social links and behavioral co-activity), stating that activity edges carry detection signal social structure alone does not, with its own measured detection-accuracy comparison against structure-only random-walk methods (SybilRank, SybilWalk) on the same datasets.

title: TrustGCN: Enabling Graph Convolutional Network for Robust Sybil Detection in OSNs
authors: Yue Sun, Zhi Yang, Yafei Dai
why_needed: Applies a graph convolutional network, trained on node features plus structure rather than structure-only propagation rules, to Sybil detection, stating a measured accuracy comparison against SybilRank and SybilBelief on the same graph; one of the earliest graph-neural-network Sybil detectors and the direct predecessor the domain brief's request for 2023-2026 GNN work is measured against.

title: Attacking Graph-Based Classification without Changing Existing Connections
authors: Xuening Xu, Xiaojiang Du, Qiang Zeng
why_needed: States an evasion attack against graph-based classifiers (the family SybilRank, SybilBelief, and GNN-based detectors all belong to) that adds only new attacker-controlled nodes and edges among them, never modifying or removing any existing honest-graph edge, and measures the resulting drop in detection accuracy; the specific critique that the constraint "the adversary cannot alter the honest graph" assumed by most Sybil-detection accuracy claims does not bound this attack.

title: Sybil Detection Using Graph Neural Networks
authors: Stuart Heeb, Andreas Plesner, Roger Wattenhofer
why_needed: SYBILGAT: applies a graph attention network that assigns learned, per-neighbor attention weights during aggregation rather than the fixed propagation weights of SybilRank/SybilBelief, evaluated on a real Twitter graph exceeding 269,000 nodes and 6.8 million edges; states a specific claim of improved robustness against a large count of attack edges, the exact failure mode of the earlier propagation-based methods, so its measured attack-edge-count-versus-accuracy curve is the number to extract.

title: More Efficient Sybil Detection Mechanisms Leveraging Resistance of Users to Attack Requests
authors: Ali Safarpoor-Dehkordi, Ahad N. Zehmakan
why_needed: Models honest users as probabilistically resistant to accepting an attack edge (rather than accepting attack requests at a fixed rate) and states a detection mechanism whose message/computation cost is measurably lower than prior random-walk mechanisms at the same accuracy, under that resistance model; a 2025 result to check against the 2013 SoK's stated gap for a targeted-attachment adversary.

title: Graph-Based Fake Account Detection: A Survey
authors: Ali Safarpoor-Dehkordi, Ahad N. Zehmakan
why_needed: A 2025 survey specifically of graph-based (including GNN-based) fake-account and Sybil detection, positioned to state which post-2013 methods it classifies as still reducible to the local-community-detection pattern Alvisi (S&P 2013) critiqued and which it considers structurally different; the freshest available systematization of this specific sub-literature.

title: SyRA: Sybil-Resilient Anonymous Signatures with Applications to Decentralized Identity
authors: Elizabeth C. Crites, Aggelos Kiayias, Markulf Kohlweiss, Amirreza Sarencheh
why_needed: A cryptographic (not graph-based) approach to Sybil resistance: each user holds one credential from an issuer and can derive unlinkable pseudonyms per context, with a signature proving pseudonym-credential consistency in zero-knowledge, so admission depends on possessing one credential rather than on graph position or a pre-trusted seed set. Directly answers the domain brief's request for a construction claiming forgery resistance without a trusted seed identity; the specific thing to check on full read is whether the credential issuer itself is a new trusted party the construction has simply relocated rather than removed. The 2024 IACR ePrint version (2024/379) predates the CCS 2025 publication.

title: De-SyRIS: A Decentralized Sybil-Resistant Identity System without a Trusted Credential Issuer
authors: Michal Ľaš, Ivan Homoliak, Juraj Mariani
why_needed: States it is the first Sybil-resistant identity system that is fully decentralized without any centralized credential issuer, combining facial-biometric verification, anti-Sybil social-graph analysis, zero-knowledge proofs, and trusted execution environments; directly targets the exact unsolved problem the domain brief states ("Sybil resistance without trusted seeds") and CRITES-CCS-25's unresolved issuer-relocation question, so the specific thing to extract on full read is which of the four named mechanisms is doing the actual trust-anchoring work and whether the trusted-execution-environment manufacturer becomes a new trusted party.

title: MeritRank: Sybil Tolerant Reputation for Merit-Based Tokenomics
authors: Bulat Nasrulin, Georgy Ishmaev, Johan Pouwelse
why_needed: Combines a decayed, feedback-weighted random-walk reputation score (subjective per-viewer, no global aggregation) with an explicit Sybil-tolerance proof bounding the reputation gain obtainable per unit of resource an attacker controls, positioned as a merit-based alternative to token-stake reputation; the closest target in this domain to a reputation construction that states a formal Sybil-resistance bound without relying on a trusted seed set, so its assumptions and proof structure are the specific things to check on full read.

title: Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router
authors: Roger Dingledine, Nick Mathewson, Paul F. Syverson
why_needed: The onion-routing construction (per-relay layered encryption, no single relay holding both origin and destination) that every tier-1 anonymity mechanism in this domain assumes or compares against. Need the original design rationale and the three-relay circuit parameter, not a secondary description.

title: Mixminion: Design of a Type III Anonymous Remailer Protocol
authors: George Danezis, Roger Dingledine, Nick Mathewson
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: The mix-network design the brief names for message-based (store-and-forward) anonymity, predating and structurally distinct from the continuous-traffic Poisson-mixing line (Loopix). Needed for a from-first-principles comparison of mix-network families, not an assumed superiority of one.

title: Private Information Retrieval
authors: Benny Chor, Oded Goldreich, Eyal Kushilevitz, Madhu Sudan
why_needed: Defines PIR itself and the multi-server (information-theoretic, non-colluding-server) construction that every single-server lattice-based PIR paper in this list positions itself against. Need the original communication-complexity bounds for k-server PIR, derived from first principles rather than assumed.

title: Software Protection and Simulation on Oblivious RAMs
authors: Oded Goldreich, Rafail Ostrovsky
why_needed: Defines Oblivious RAM and proves the original bandwidth-multiplier lower bound the brief asks about; every later ORAM construction (Path ORAM, etc.) states its overhead against this bound. Needed to state the multiplier as a derived quantity rather than a recalled folk number.

title: Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications
authors: Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
why_needed: Introduces the distributed point function (DPF) primitive underlying every multi-server PIR and PIR-based metadata-private-messaging scheme in this list (Talek, Pung's successors, Express). Need the construction and its key-size/communication bound, since the brief explicitly asks for DPF-based multi-server PIR.

title: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
authors: Payap Sirinam, Mohsen Imani, Marc Juarez, Matthew Wright
why_needed: The deep-learning classifier that the prior pass's headline numbers (98% vs undefended, 90%+ vs WTF-PAD, reduced to 49.7% by Walkie-Talkie) are attributed to. Every one of those figures must be re-derived from this paper's own tables, with dataset size, closed/open-world setting, and number of monitored sites stated — the prior-pass error pattern applies directly here.

title: Toward an Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense
authors: Marc Juarez, Mohsen Imani, Mike Perry, Claudia Diaz, Matthew Wright
why_needed: The WTF-PAD defense paper itself. The prior pass cites its overhead as a range (32-54%) without stating which experimental condition each end of the range corresponds to; that must come from this paper's own measurement tables, not a repeated range.

title: Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting
authors: Tao Wang, Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg
why_needed: This is the Walkie-Talkie paper, cited in the prior pass and the brief by that name only; need the actual title and the paper's own reported classifier-accuracy-under-defense figure and its overhead, since 'Walkie-Talkie' is a name, not a citation.

title: A Systematic Approach to Developing and Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Defenses
authors: Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Tao Wang, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg
why_needed: This is the Tamaraw paper (constant-rate padding, named in the brief by mechanism name only). Need the actual per-direction rate and burst-alignment parameters and the measured bandwidth overhead against the closed-world classifier used, as a fixed-rate padding baseline against which later adaptive defenses (RegulaTor, Surakav, FRONT) state their improvement.

title: Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting
authors: Jiajun Gong, Tao Wang
why_needed: This is the FRONT defense (front-loaded padding). Need its own measured overhead-versus-classifier-accuracy tradeoff curve, since the brief lists it as a distinct 2020 defense to compare against Walkie-Talkie's 2014 numbers and the 2022-2024 defenses below.

title: RegulaTor: A Straightforward Website Fingerprinting Defense
authors: James K. Holland, Nicholas Hopper
why_needed: A 2022 defense the prior pass never mentions. Its own paper reports overhead-versus-defended-accuracy figures against Deep Fingerprinting, WTF-PAD, and FRONT on a common dataset; those numbers are the currency check the brief requires for a field that 'moved fast.'

title: Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense
authors: Jiajun Gong, Wuqi Zhang, Charles Zhang, Tao Wang
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: A GAN-based trace-generation defense, competing directly with FRONT (same lead author, later paper) and RegulaTor. Need its measured accuracy-versus-overhead numbers against Deep Fingerprinting to place it correctly relative to the others on the same axis.

title: Real-Time Website Fingerprinting Defense via Traffic Cluster Anonymization
authors: Meng Shen, Kexin Ji, Jinhe Wu, Qi Li, Xiangdong Kong, Ke Xu, Liehuang Zhu
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: A 2024 defense at the top security venue, satisfying the brief's explicit requirement for 2023-2026 website-fingerprinting defenses. Need its measured latency overhead (the paper's 'real-time' and 'zero-delay' claims recur across this literature and must be checked against each paper's own definition of delay).

title: Countmamba: A Generalized Website Fingerprinting Attack via Coarse-Grained Representation and Fine-Grained Prediction
authors: Xianwen Deng, Ruijie Zhao, Yanhao Wang, Mingwei Zhan, Zhi Xue, Yijun Wang
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: A 2025 attack, satisfying the brief's explicit requirement to include 2024-2026 work rather than treating Deep Fingerprinting (2018) as the current state of the art. Need to check whether its reported accuracy against the current defenses (RegulaTor, Surakav, FRONT) supersedes the 2018-2020 attack-defense numbers the prior pass relied on.

title: The Loopix Anonymity System
authors: Ania M. Piotrowska, Jamie Hayes, Tariq Elahi, Sebastian Meiser, George Danezis
why_needed: The Poisson-mixing, per-hop independent-exponential-delay design that Nym deploys. Need the paper's own throughput-per-relay and end-to-end latency distribution (not a single summary number) and the exact loop-cover-traffic rate parameter, since the prior pass's 'upward of 300 messages per second... under 1.5 ms' figures must be checked against the paper's stated experimental topology.

title: Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis
authors: Jelle van den Hooff, David Lazar, Matei Zaharia, Nickolai Zeldovich
why_needed: The differential-privacy-noise mixing design that the Stadium/Karaoke/Yodel line (same MIT group, successive papers) each state their improvement against. Need Vuvuzela's own measured latency and per-server dead-drop throughput as the baseline those later papers compare to.

title: Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System
authors: Nirvan Tyagi, Yossi Gilad, Derek Leung, Matei Zaharia, Nickolai Zeldovich
why_needed: States itself as scaling Vuvuzela's single-server-pair design to many servers via verifiable shuffling. Need its own measured throughput scaling with server count, and the exact security assumption (number of honest servers required) it needs, which differs from Vuvuzela's two-server assumption.

title: Karaoke: Distributed Private Messaging Immune to Passive Traffic Analysis
authors: David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich
why_needed: States a latency improvement over Vuvuzela and Stadium by batching multiple rounds together; need the paper's own measured latency-versus-user-count curve to check whether that improvement is asymptotic or a constant-factor result tied to a specific deployment size.

title: Yodel: Strong Metadata Security for Voice Calls
authors: David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich
why_needed: Same group's follow-on to Karaoke, targeting voice-call latency budgets (tens of milliseconds) rather than message latency (seconds). Need its own round-trip latency figure to determine whether any mix-network construction in this line meets an interactive-latency bar, directly relevant to the brief's open 'private search at interactive latency' question, generalized to interactive communication.

title: Talek: Private Group Messaging with Hidden Access Patterns
authors: Raymond Cheng, William Scott, Elisaweta Masserova, Irene Zhang, Vipul Goyal, Thomas E. Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Bryan Parno
why_needed: A PIR-based (not mix-based) approach to hiding who-reads-what in group messaging, giving a distinct point of comparison against the differential-privacy-noise family (Vuvuzela/Stadium/Karaoke/Yodel). Need its measured per-message server computation cost to compare directly against the PIR throughput figures in this same domain.

title: Studying the Anonymity Trilemma with a Discrete-event Mix Network Simulator
authors: Ania M. Piotrowska
why_needed: An independent, simulator-based empirical comparison of three deployed mix networks (Elixxir, HOPR, Nym) against the trilemma bound, by the original Loopix author. This is the paper to cite for Nym's actual deployed anonymity/latency/bandwidth tradeoff, since Nym itself has no peer-reviewed measurement paper (Nym's public materials are project documentation, not primary evidence per rule 1).

title: PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing
authors: Sebastian Angel, Hao Chen, Kim Laine, Srinath T. V. Setty
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: This is the SealPIR paper. The prior pass states its throughput as '102 MB/s' with no experimental condition attached; need the paper's own hardware description, database size, and single- versus multi-thread setting, since the brief flags this whole area as one where 'the prior pass's numbers are likely stale.'

title: OnionPIR: Response Efficient Single-Server PIR
authors: Muhammad Haris Mughees, Hao Chen, Ling Ren
why_needed: States an improvement over SealPIR specifically in response size (the client-side download), a different axis than server throughput. Need the paper's own response-size-versus-database-size table to compare against Spiral's response size on the same axis.

title: Spiral: Fast, High-Rate Single-Server PIR via FHE Composition
authors: Samir Jordan Menon, David J. Wu
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: The prior pass's tier-3 selection at '310 MB/s, 14 kB query, 84 kB response, 24.5 s server computation on a 7.9 GB database.' Full text confirmed retrievable (spot-checked: 46 pages at eprint.iacr.org/2022/368.pdf) and states exactly this scenario; next-pass extraction must pull the full table across database sizes, not only the headline row, and must check that table against SimplePIR/DoublePIR's throughput on the same database sizes.

title: One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
authors: Alexandra Henzinger, Matthew M. Hong, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Sarah Meiklejohn, Vinod Vaikuntanathan
why_needed: This single paper defines both SimplePIR and DoublePIR, named in the brief as separate systems; need the actual relationship (DoublePIR trades some of SimplePIR's throughput for a much smaller client-held hint) and the paper's own throughput numbers, since the prior pass says only 'SimplePIR reaches higher throughput and requires the client to download a large precomputed hint first' without a number for either the throughput or the hint size.

title: Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation
authors: Mingxun Zhou, Andrew Park, Wenting Zheng, Elaine Shi
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: Claims sublinear (rather than linear) server computation per query after preprocessing, which if it holds directly attacks the brief's open problem 4 ('current single-server PIR costs seconds per query on multi-gigabyte databases'). Need the paper's own per-query server-time figure after amortized preprocessing, and the preprocessing cost it is amortized against, since a sublinear-per-query claim with an expensive un-amortized preprocessing step is a different claim from true interactive-latency PIR.

title: YPIR: High-Throughput Single-Server PIR with Silent Preprocessing
authors: Samir Jordan Menon, David J. Wu
why_needed: A 2024 follow-on to Spiral by the same authors, explicitly named by the brief's '2023-2026 PIR result' requirement. 'Silent preprocessing' is a specific claim (no interaction needed to generate preprocessing material) that must be checked against what SimplePIR/DoublePIR's 'hint download' actually requires, since the two papers may be making incompatible claims about what round trip is eliminated.

title: FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
authors: Alex Davidson, Goncalo Pestana, Sofia Celi
why_needed: A 2023 single-server PIR result built on plain LWE rather than ring-LWE (unlike Spiral/OnionPIR), trading response size for a simpler security assumption. Need its own throughput and per-client preprocessed-database-size figures to place on the same axis as SimplePIR/Piano/YPIR.

title: Efficient Batched Oblivious PRF with Applications to Private Set Intersection
authors: Vladimir Kolesnikov, Ranjit Kumaresan, Mike Rosulek, Ni Trieu
why_needed: The OPRF-based PSI construction (commonly cited as KKRT) that the prior pass's own SPLiNTERNET-integration document names as 'the fix path' for replacing salted-hash PSI. Need this paper's own measured per-element cost and total running time at a stated set size, since it is being relied on as an actual replacement mechanism, not only a name.

title: Private Set Intersection in the Internet Setting From Lightweight Oblivious PRF
authors: Melissa Chase, Peihan Miao
why_needed: States an improvement over KKRT specifically for the unbalanced, high-latency-network setting (one large set on a server, one small set from a client) which is the relevant setting for a client querying a network peer, as opposed to KKRT's original two-comparable-sized-set, low-latency LAN setting. Need its own measured communication and running-time figures at the set-size asymmetry it targets.

title: Access Pattern disclosure on Searchable Encryption: Ramification, Attack and Mitigation
authors: Mohammad Saiful Islam, Mehmet Kuzu, Murat Kantarcioglu
why_needed: The first of the three SSE leakage-abuse attack papers the brief names by author surname only. Need the actual attack mechanism (co-occurrence pattern matching against a known-plaintext reference distribution) and its stated auxiliary-knowledge requirement, to state precisely what SSE reveals beyond 'match/no-match.'

title: Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption
authors: David Cash, Paul Grubbs, Jason Perry, Thomas Ristenpart
why_needed: The second of the three named leakage-abuse attacks, generalizing Islam-Kuzu-Kantarcioglu to a wider class of SSE schemes and a formal leakage-profile framework. Need the paper's own count-attack and file-injection-attack success rates at stated auxiliary-knowledge fractions.

title: Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks
authors: Paul Grubbs, Marie-Sarah Lacharite, Brice Minaud, Kenneth G. Paterson
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: The third named leakage-abuse attack, reframing query and value reconstruction as a statistical learning problem to give reconstruction guarantees under weaker assumptions than the two prior attacks. Need its stated bound on the auxiliary-distribution assumption strength required, which determines how easy the attack is against a realistic peer holding real-world data.

title: Path ORAM: An Extremely Simple Oblivious RAM Protocol
authors: Emil Stefanov, Marten van Dijk, Elaine Shi, Christopher W. Fletcher, Ling Ren, Xiangyao Yu, Srinivas Devadas
why_needed: The ORAM construction actually deployed in practice and cited as the reference point for 'the bandwidth multiplier' the prior pass states as 10-100x with no derivation. Need the paper's own asymptotic bandwidth blowup formula (as a function of the client-side stash size and tree depth) so that figure is derived rather than recalled.

title: Yes, There is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!
authors: Kasper Green Larsen, Jesper Buus Nielsen
why_needed: Proves an Omega(log n) bandwidth-overhead lower bound for statistically secure ORAM, closing a gap left open by earlier work that only had lower bounds for restricted ORAM classes. This is the structural ceiling against which any claimed low-overhead ORAM construction must be checked, directly relevant to whether the brief's ORAM bandwidth multiplier can ever be reduced below a logarithmic factor.

title: Dissent: Accountable Anonymous Group Messaging
authors: Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Bryan Ford
why_needed: The dining-cryptographers-network (DC-net) based anonymous-broadcast system the brief names first. Need its own measured per-round latency and message throughput as a function of group size, since the brief states DC-net coordination cost 'grows with group size' as an unquantified claim from the prior pass that must be replaced with the paper's actual scaling figure.

title: Herbivore: A Scalable and Efficient Protocol for Anonymous Communication
authors: Sharad Goel, Mark Robson, Milo Polte, Emin Gun Sirer
venue: Cornell University Computer Science Technical Report 2003-1890
why_needed: Not indexed on DBLP or Crossref (confirmed absent from both; it is a technical report, not a peer-reviewed venue publication), but institutionally archived at Cornell eCommons. Its clique-partitioning approach to DC-nets (fixed clique size k, 3k-user cap per clique) is the scaling mechanism named alongside Dissent and Riposte in the brief and needs its own measured bandwidth/latency figures at a stated clique size.

title: Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users
authors: Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Dan Boneh, David Mazieres
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: States an improvement over Dissent/Herbivore-style DC-nets by using a write-only PIR-like scheme (distributed point functions again, connecting back to Gilboa-Ishai) instead of pairwise DC-net coordination, claiming the 'millions of users' scale in its title. Need the paper's own measured server-side computation and bandwidth cost per round at a stated user count, to check that scaling claim against Dissent's group-size-dependent cost.

title: On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees
authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt, Jon Millican, Kevin Milner
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Introduces Asynchronous Ratcheting Trees (ART), the binary-tree key-derivation structure that TreeKEM and BeeKEM both belong to per BeeKEM's own classification. This is the first formal security treatment of tree-structured group key derivation and the definitions of forward secrecy and post-compromise security it uses are the ones the rest of the CGKA line inherits or revises.

title: TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups
authors: Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Richard Barnes, Eric Rescorla
why_needed: The original TreeKEM proposal submitted to the IETF MLS working group: the binary-tree public-key structure where each node's key is derivable from its children, later standardized into RFC 9420. Not indexed on DBLP (a technical report, not a venue paper); verified only against the HAL landing page and the citation string inside BeeKEM's own bibliography.

title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol
authors: Richard Barnes, Benjamin Beurdouche, Raphael Robert, Jon Millican, Emad Omara, Katriel Cohn-Gordon
why_needed: The standardized wire protocol for tree-based continuous group key agreement with a centralized delivery service imposing total order. Every decentralized construction in this domain (DCGKA, BeeKEM, DeCAF) states its contribution as removing this total-order requirement, so the requirement itself must be sourced from the standard that imposes it.

title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Architecture
authors: Benjamin Beurdouche, Eric Rescorla, Emad Omara, Srinivas Inguva, Alan Duric
why_needed: Describes the deployment architecture around RFC 9420: the Delivery Service and Authentication Service roles, how membership changes are proposed and committed, and where the centralization point sits that a decentralized construction must remove or replace.

title: Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging
authors: Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Yevgeniy Dodis, Yiannis Tselekounis
why_needed: First formal cryptographic security proof for the MLS/TreeKEM draft, identifying gaps between the informally claimed and formally provable security properties of tree-based CGKA. This is the baseline every later formal-security paper on MLS (Alwen TCC 2020, Klein S&P 2021, Wallez S&P 2025) compares against.

title: Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security
authors: Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Daniel Jost, Marta Mularczyk
why_needed: Defines the CGKA security game against an active (not just passive) adversary who can inject malicious messages, the model that BeeKEM's own security proofs (ki-DCGKA game) build on and extend to the decentralized, non-totally-ordered setting.

title: On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols
authors: Alexander Bienstock, Yevgeniy Dodis, Paul Rösler
why_needed: Proves lower bounds on the communication and computation cost a group ratcheting protocol must pay to tolerate concurrent updates, the theoretical origin of the O(n)-vs-O(log n) tension that CoCoA, Fork-Resilient CGKA, DeCAF and BeeKEM each attempt to narrow from a different direction.

title: Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement
authors: Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Michael Walter, Chethan Kamath, Margarita Capretto, Miguel Cueto, Ilia Markov, Michelle Yeo, Joël Alwen, Krzysztof Pietrzak
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
why_needed: First CGKA construction with a security proof against an adaptive adversary who chooses which parties to corrupt based on protocol transcripts already seen, closing a gap the CRYPTO 2020 and TCC 2020 proofs left open (they assumed static or non-adaptive corruption).

title: CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement
authors: Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak, Michael Walter
why_needed: A centralized-delivery-service CGKA construction (still requires total order) that tolerates concurrent updates within one epoch at sub-O(n) cost rather than serializing them, the comparison point for BeeKEM's own concurrency handling under partition.

title: On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA
authors: Alexander Bienstock, Yevgeniy Dodis, Sanjam Garg, Garrison Grogan, Mohammad Hajiabadi, Paul Rösler
why_needed: Proves that no CGKA protocol built black-box from standard public-key encryption can achieve sublinear-in-group-size communication cost in the worst case, holding even in an offline setting where the sequence of group operations is known in advance. This is the specific impossibility result that 'Fair-Weather No More' (2026) narrows and that bears directly on whether BeeKEM's O(log n)-common-case/O(n)-worst-case split, and its retention-parameter tradeoff, are inherent to any decentralized construction or specific to BeeKEM's choice of primitives.

title: A Concrete Treatment of Efficient Continuous Group Key Agreement via Multi-Recipient PKEs
authors: Keitaro Hashimoto, Shuichi Katsumata, Eamonn W. Postlethwaite, Thomas Prest, Bas Westerbaan
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Replaces TreeKEM's pairwise per-node public-key encryptions with a single multi-recipient ciphertext, an alternative cost-reduction mechanism to BeeKEM's tree-and-CRDT approach, still under a centralized delivery service. Gives independent concrete (not just asymptotic) bandwidth figures for the same update operation BeeKEM measures.

title: How to Hide MetaData in MLS-Like Secure Group Messaging: Simple, Modular, and Post-Quantum
authors: Keitaro Hashimoto, Shuichi Katsumata, Thomas Prest
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: A generic wrapper that upgrades a non-metadata-hiding CGKA (including TreeKEM and, by the same argument, BeeKEM) into one that hides membership metadata from the delivery infrastructure, and states explicitly that the wrapper composes with post-quantum key-encapsulation. Directly addresses both the metadata-privacy and post-quantum requirements of this domain in one mechanism.

title: Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement
authors: Joël Alwen, Marta Mularczyk, Yiannis Tselekounis
why_needed: Defines Fork-Resilience for CGKA under a centralized delivery service that can be made to present different group histories to different members, the same forking threat model BeeKEM's Cross-Fork Security targets for the fully decentralized case with no delivery service at all. The precise formal definition here is what BeeKEM's Cross-Fork Security proof must be checked against for consistency or divergence.

title: TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security
authors: Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Benjamin Beurdouche, Karthikeyan Bhargavan
why_needed: A machine-checked (F*, DY*) formal specification and proof of the MLS sub-protocol that governs adding, removing, and updating members and keeping every member's view of the group state consistent and authenticated. This is the administered-group-membership half of MLS that a decentralized replacement (BeeKEM's operation-graph replay) must reproduce the guarantees of without a central authority. Distinguished Paper Award at USENIX Security 2023.

title: Cryptographic Administration for Secure Group Messaging
authors: David Balbás, Daniel Collins, Serge Vaudenay
why_needed: Formalizes administrated group messaging, where designated administrators (not every member) can add or remove members and their permissions are themselves cryptographically enforced rather than assumed. Directly on point for the domain's 'administrated and decentralized group membership' axis: states the security definitions and cost of the administrated end of that axis against which any fully peer-symmetric decentralized scheme must be compared.

title: WhatsUpp with Sender Keys? Analysis, Improvements and Security Proofs
authors: David Balbás, Daniel Collins, Phillip Gajland
why_needed: First formal cryptographic model and security proof for Sender Keys, the pairwise-fan-out group-encryption scheme deployed in WhatsApp and Signal, and proposes a modification lowering its total communication cost from quadratic to linear in group size. Also posted to arXiv as 2301.07045. This is the primary source for the Sender Keys O(n^2) cost claim in this domain, which must be cited to this paper rather than stated from memory.

title: Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
authors: Martin R. Albrecht, Sofía Celi, Benjamin Dowling, Daniel Jones
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
why_needed: Finds and demonstrates exploitable key-confusion and unauthenticated-key-share attacks in the deployed Matrix federated messaging protocol's group-session key-sharing mechanism, a real federated (partially decentralized) group-membership system distinct from the MLS/TreeKEM/DCGKA line. Gives independent evidence of what fails in a real deployed decentralized-adjacent group-key mechanism, as opposed to a paper-only threat model.

title: DeCAF: Decentralizable CGKA with Fast Healing
authors: Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak
why_needed: A second, independent decentralized CGKA construction from the Alwen/Pietrzak line, explicitly positioned against Weidner et al.'s DCGKA on healing speed after a compromise. This is the direct competing result to both DCGKA and BeeKEM that the domain brief names by mechanism family, and its cost and healing-time figures are the other side's numbers that BeeKEM's comparison table must be checked against.

title: Quarantined-TreeKEM: A Continuous Group Key Agreement for MLS, Secure in Presence of Inactive Users
authors: Céline Chevalier, Guirec Lebrun, Ange Martinelli, Abdul Rahman Taleb
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Modifies TreeKEM to remain secure and continue admitting updates when some members are inactive (offline, not merely slow) for extended periods without excluding them from the group, a direct analogue under a centralized delivery service of the partition-tolerance problem BeeKEM solves in the fully decentralized case. The inactive-member cost figures are a comparison point for BeeKEM's own new-member catch-up cost.
