title: Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates Without Pruning
authors: Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Boran Erol, Krzysztof Pietrzak
why_needed: A propose-and-commit variant of TreeKEM (centralized delivery service) that keeps update cost at Θ(log N) under a moderate rate of concurrent update proposals per commit, without the tree-pruning step earlier schemes needed. Published after BeeKEM's ePrint posting is dated; a direct, recent comparison point for the concurrency-cost figures BeeKEM reports for the decentralized case.

title: TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security
authors: Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Karthikeyan Bhargavan
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
why_needed: A machine-checked symbolic (not just computational) security analysis of the full TreeKEM protocol as standardized, extending the TreeSync formal-methods line to the key-agreement core itself. Published in 2025, after the RFC finalized and after most of the computational-model proofs in this domain, so it is the paper to check for any gap the computational proofs missed.

title: Analyzing Group Chat Encryption in MLS, Session, Signal, and Matrix
authors: Joseph Jaeger, Akshaya Kumar
why_needed: A single unified formal analysis comparing four deployed group-messaging protocols with different membership-administration and delivery-service architectures (MLS's tree-based centralized delivery service, Session's and Signal's Sender-Keys-derived designs, and Matrix's federated design) under one security model. This is the paper to cite for a cross-protocol comparison rather than reasoning from any one protocol's own claims about the others.

title: Tighter Provable Security for TreeKEM
authors: Karen Azari, Andreas Ellison
why_needed: Improves the concrete (not just asymptotic) security bound of the CRYPTO 2020 and TCC 2020 proofs for TreeKEM, which changes the key sizes needed for a given security level. Any concrete-parameter comparison between TreeKEM-family and BeeKEM at matched security levels needs this bound rather than the older, looser ones.

title: Making Post Quantum Key Exchange Efficient: An Implementation with the MLS Protocol
authors: Noah Greene, Britta Hale
why_needed: First benchmarking of hybrid classical/post-quantum ciphersuite combinations inside an actual MLS implementation, measured across group size, CPU cycles, message bytes, and wall-clock runtime, and reports overhead savings against naive post-quantum-only ciphersuites. This supplies measured post-quantum cost figures for the tree-based line that BeeKEM^PQ (sketched, not benchmarked, in the BeeKEM paper) can be checked against.

title: Generic Anonymity Wrapper for Messaging Protocols
authors: Lea Thiemt, Paul Rösler, Alexander Bienstock, Rolfe Schmidt, Yevgeniy Dodis
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: Formalizes an Authenticated Anonymity Wrapper that hides sender/recipient metadata for both two-party and group messaging protocols with forward anonymity and post-compromise anonymity, states it gives stronger anonymity guarantees than Sender Keys achieves natively, and the paper states Signal is evaluating deployment. Signal's own evaluation is a claim to attribute to Signal if repeated, not to be stated as fact from this paper alone. A second, independent metadata-hiding mechanism for group messaging beyond the CCS 2022 wrapper, letting the two be compared on cost and threat model.

title: Bots can Snoop: Uncovering and Mitigating Privacy Risks of Bots in Group Chats
authors: Kai-Hsiang Chou, Yi-Min Lin, Yi-An Wang, Jonathan Weiping Li, Tiffany Hyun-Jin Kim, Hsu-Chun Hsiao
why_needed: Measures the privacy exposure created when a third-party bot is added as a full group member in existing group-messaging deployments (it receives every message any tree-based or Sender-Keys scheme delivers to a member) and proposes SnoopGuard, a tree-based CGKA extended with selective Internal Group Anonymity so a member's identity can be hidden from specific other members, including bots, without excluding them from the group. Bears on any design that treats 'group member' as a single undifferentiated access class.

title: Decentralized Continuous Group Key Agreement for UAV Ad-Hoc Network
authors: Hong, Zhou, Yang, Shen, Zheng (full given names not resolved from Crossref metadata)
venue: Machine Learning for Cyber Security (ML4CS), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
why_needed: Applies decentralized CGKA specifically to an unmanned-aerial-vehicle ad-hoc network, a deployment setting where network partition from mobility and range is the normal operating condition rather than an edge case. Directly relevant to whether BeeKEM's conjectured retention-parameter tradeoff between cross-branch recovery and forward secrecy holds up against measurements from a real partition-prone physical network, as opposed to a simulated one.

title: Amigo: Secure Group Mesh Messaging in Realistic Protest Settings
authors: David Inyangson, Sarah Radway, Tushar M. Jois, Nelly Fazio, James Mickens
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
why_needed: A group-messaging design for Bluetooth-range mesh networks (no internet, no central server, frequent partition) evaluated under a protest threat model, the most physically decentralized deployment setting in this domain. Its group-key mechanism and measured costs under partition and device churn are the comparison point for whether BeeKEM-style designs, built for internet-connected causal broadcast, extend to a fully offline mesh.

title: Auditable Continuous Group Key Agreement
authors: Easwar Vivek Mangipudi, Maddie Gorman, Sasha Levinshteyn
why_needed: Posted after BeeKEM. Adds an auditability extension to CGKA with a Rust prototype and a post-quantum custom multi-stage STARK proof system, targeting adaptive post-quantum security in the secure-erasure model. Directly answers the domain brief's instruction to seek anything published after BeeKEM, and is a second post-quantum decentralized-adjacent CGKA construction to compare against BeeKEM^PQ.

title: Fair-Weather No More: Guaranteed Efficiency in Secure Group Messaging
authors: James Bartusek, Nir Bitansky, Yevgeniy Dodis, Rachit Garg, David J. Wu
why_needed: Posted after BeeKEM. Presents the first CGKA protocol with provably logarithmic WORST-CASE (not just common-case) complexity, based on a falsifiable post-quantum assumption (decomposed LWE), achieving post-compromise security but not forward secrecy in the base construction, and forward secrecy only at the cost of a linear-time refresh in a random-oracle extension. Its abstract states this narrows, but does not close, the gap the CRYPTO/TCC 2022 impossibility results (Bienstock et al.) opened. This is the single most direct available answer to the domain brief's question of whether BeeKEM's retention-parameter tradeoff is inherent: it shows worst-case-sublinear CGKA is possible in principle but that forward secrecy still forces a linear-cost operation somewhere, from a completely different (complexity-theoretic, not partition-tolerance) angle than BeeKEM's own conjecture.

title: Benchmarking of the Amortized Post Quantum Combiner for MLS
authors: Britta Hale, Tian, Wang (given names not resolved from Crossref metadata)
venue: Security Standardisation Research (SSR), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
why_needed: Measures the amortized cost of a hybrid classical/post-quantum key combiner integrated into MLS across repeated group operations, rather than a single-operation snapshot. A second, independent post-quantum-MLS cost measurement (after Greene and Hale 2025) from an overlapping author, useful for checking whether the 2025 single-run figures hold up amortized over a session.

title: A Formal Security Analysis of the Signal Messaging Protocol
authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Benjamin Dowling, Luke Garratt, Douglas Stebila
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P); extended version Journal of Cryptology 2020
why_needed: The formal security proof of the Double Ratchet as used in two-party Signal sessions, defining the forward-secrecy and post-compromise-security properties in the specific asynchronous, out-of-order-delivery setting that group protocols must also handle. Sender Keys and every pairwise-fan-out group scheme (WhatsApp, early Signal groups) is built from pairwise Double Ratchet sessions between this protocol's endpoints, so its guarantees and failure modes are inherited claims, not independent ones, for the group case.

title: On Post-Compromise Security
authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt
why_needed: Coins and formally defines Post-Compromise Security: the guarantee that a party recovers security after a key compromise once it takes further protocol steps, without needing to detect the compromise first. Every later paper in this domain that claims 'post-compromise security' (DCGKA, BeeKEM included) is claiming this specific, cited definition, not an informal synonym for 'heals eventually.'

title: SoK: Secure Messaging
authors: Nik Unger, Sergej Dechand, Joseph Bonneau, Sascha Fahl, Henning Perl, Ian Goldberg, Matthew Smith
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
why_needed: Systematization of Knowledge covering the secure-messaging landscape as of 2015, including the trust-establishment, conversation-security, and transport-privacy properties every later group-messaging paper in this domain positions itself against. Predates MLS and the CGKA line, so it establishes the pre-existing terminology and evaluation criteria (rather than criteria invented by any single later paper) that a Pareto-style comparison in this project should reuse or explicitly justify departing from.

title: Rollercoaster: An Efficient Group-Multicast Scheme for Mix Networks
authors: Daniel Hugenroth, Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford
why_needed: From the same author group as DCGKA (Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford), this paper covers the metadata-privacy half the domain brief asks for: an efficient scheme for delivering group-multicast ciphertexts through a mix network so the network operator cannot learn group membership or message timing correlations from delivery traffic, complementary to (not a replacement for) the key-agreement mechanism itself.

title: Mesh Messaging in Large-Scale Protests: Breaking Bridgefy
authors: Martin R. Albrecht, Jorge Blasco, Rikke Bjerg Jensen, Lenka Mareková
why_needed: Demonstrates concrete message-forgery, denial-of-service, and user-deanonymization attacks against Bridgefy, a deployed Bluetooth-mesh messaging application used during real protests, caused by its complete absence of end-to-end encryption or authenticated group key agreement in its group/broadcast messages at the time of the study. Establishes, as a measured fact from a real deployment rather than a hypothetical, what specifically fails when a mesh-network messaging app ships without the cryptographic mechanisms the rest of this domain provides.

title: Non-Interactive Key Exchange
authors: Eduarda S. V. Freire, Dennis Hofheinz, Eike Kiltz, Kenneth G. Paterson
why_needed: Formally defines Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE): a scheme where two parties compute a shared key from each other's static public key alone, with no protocol messages exchanged. BeeKEM's core mechanism (each inner tree node's secret is derived by NIKE between its two children) is built directly on this primitive and its security definition; the strength of BeeKEM's proofs is bounded by the strength of the NIKE security notion this paper supplies.

title: Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
authors: Bram Cohen
venue: Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (presented at IPTPS 2003)
why_needed: The design document for BitTorrent's tit-for-tat choking algorithm: reciprocal upload allocation among the four best-uploading peers plus one optimistic unchoke slot, argued as approximating pareto-efficient exchange. Every attack paper in this domain (Piatek, Locher, Sirivianos, Levin) targets this exact mechanism, so its precise rule set is the baseline every exploit is measured against.

title: Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?
authors: Michael Piatek, Tomas Isdal, Thomas E. Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Arun Venkataramani
why_needed: Builds BitTyrant, a strategic client that reallocates upload toward peers with the best return-per-byte and reports a median 70% download-throughput gain on live swarms for a 1 Mbit/s connection; the paper this pass's own earlier draft cited from a secondary summary, so the primary text's exact experimental conditions (connection speed, swarm sample, measurement method) must be extracted directly rather than repeated from any prior document including this project's own CLAUDE.md.

title: Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap
authors: Thomas Locher, Patrick Moor, Stefan Schmid, Roger Wattenhofer
why_needed: Introduces BitThief, a client that completes downloads while uploading nothing at all by exploiting optimistic unchoking and connecting to many more peers than the reference client does; the mechanism defeated (optimistic unchoke as the sole non-reciprocal admission path) is a specific, checkable property distinct from BitTyrant's exploit of the reciprocal-allocation formula.

title: Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit
authors: Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Rex Chen, Xiaowei Yang
why_needed: A third, independent free-riding construction against the same tit-for-tat mechanism, obtained by connecting to an inflated set of tracker-reported peers to raise the chance of receiving an optimistic unchoke; needed to check whether its measured completion rate and required peer-set size agree with or exceed BitThief's, since the brief requires presenting disagreeing numbers from independent papers side by side rather than picking one.

title: BitTorrent is an Auction: Analyzing and Improving BitTorrent's Incentives
authors: Dave Levin, Katrina LaCurts, Neil Spring, Bobby Bhattacharjee
why_needed: Models the choking mechanism as a first-price auction, shows the model predicts measured behavior of deployed clients, and proposes PropShare, proportional-share upload allocation, as a replacement; needed as the measured comparison point against Cohen's original tit-for-tat rule and against BitTyrant's exploit, since PropShare is presented as a fix rather than only an attack.

title: Free Riding on Gnutella
authors: Eytan Adar, Bernardo A. Huberman
why_needed: The original measurement establishing that a large share of Gnutella participants share no files while consuming search and download bandwidth from the rest, from a trace of actual client traffic; the number every later free-riding measurement paper positions itself against, and needed in full text since abstracts of this paper are known to be quoted with rounded or misattributed percentages elsewhere in this field's literature.

title: Free Riding on Gnutella Revisited: The Bell Tolls?
authors: Daniel Hughes, Geoff Coulson, James Walkerdine
why_needed: An independent re-measurement of Gnutella free-riding five years after Adar and Huberman, needed to check whether the original fraction held, rose, or fell as the network and client population changed; this is the exact kind of independent-measurement paper the brief prioritizes because it is titled after its own contribution rather than the mechanism, making it easy to miss by keyword search alone.

title: The Virtual Commons: Why Free-Riding Can Be Tolerated in File Sharing Networks
authors: Ramayya Krishnan, Michael D. Smith, Zhulei Tang, Rahul Telang
why_needed: An analytic model concluding that consumption-without-contribution does not collapse aggregate download performance below a stated bound under stated conditions on demand and peer population growth; this is a measured/derived structural claim to extract on its own terms, kept separate from the value judgment (common elsewhere in this literature) that free-riding is a defect to be engineered away regardless of its measured effect on throughput.

title: KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing
authors: Vivek Vishnumurthy, Sangeeth Chandrakumar, Emin Gün Sirer
venue: Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PEcon)
why_needed: Defines a distributed scalar credit balance (karma) maintained by a replicated bank-set of nodes selected by consistent hashing over each participant's identifier, tolerant of a stated fraction of malicious bank-set members, increased on contribution and decreased on consumption; the currency/credit-scheme family member the brief names directly, and the account structure every later credit or token scheme in this domain is compared against.

title: Samsara: Honor Among Thieves in Peer-to-Peer Storage
authors: Landon P. Cox, Brian D. Noble
why_needed: Enforces symmetric storage exchange without payment or certified identity by requiring each storage claimant to hold a matching claim from the peer it stores for, backed by forced periodic proof-of-possession challenges and a punitive reclamation mechanism when a peer holding a claim disappears; needed as the storage-specific incentive design distinct from a fungible credit system, and as the source of its measured proof-of-possession overhead and its stated failure condition when both peers in an exchange pair vanish simultaneously.

title: Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives
authors: Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Xiaowei Yang, Stanislaw Jarecki
why_needed: Withholds the decryption key for a content block from a downloader until that downloader has itself uploaded a matching amount to others, stated by the authors to be provably non-manipulable unlike BitTorrent's choking heuristic; needed to extract the exact provable-non-manipulability claim and its assumption set, since it is cited elsewhere in this project only from a one-line paraphrase and the assumption set determines whether the same proof survives an open, identity-free membership model.

title: Incentives for Sharing in Peer-to-Peer Networks
authors: Philippe Golle, Kevin Leyton-Brown, Ilya Mironov
why_needed: A game-theoretic model of a file-sharing network as a population of agents choosing a contribution level, deriving the Nash equilibria under a stated set of payoff structures and identifying which payoff structures make full free-riding the unique equilibrium; needed as the earliest formal mechanism-design treatment of consumption-without-contribution the brief asks for, giving the equilibrium-selection argument later empirical papers either confirm or contradict.

title: Free-Riding and Whitewashing in Peer-to-Peer Systems
authors: Michal Feldman, Christos H. Papadimitriou, John Chuang, Ion Stoica
venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
why_needed: Formalizes whitewashing, discarding an identifier with a poor standing and rejoining under a fresh one, as a distinct failure mode from ordinary free-riding, and derives conditions under which a reciprocity mechanism remains incentive-compatible when identity is free to discard; this is the mechanism-design result that determines whether any credit or reputation scheme in this domain survives a Sybil-free but pseudonym-free membership model, which is exactly the membership model an identity-light decentralized system would use.

title: Enforcing Fair Sharing of Peer-to-Peer Resources
authors: Tsuen-Wan Ngan, Dan S. Wallach, Peter Druschel
why_needed: A second, contemporaneous storage-fairness construction alongside Samsara, enforcing a global storage-consumption limit per participant via auditable, cryptographically linked storage claims distributed across the system rather than pairwise symmetric exchange; needed as the direct architectural alternative to Samsara so the comparison in the brief's per-component selection step (pairwise-symmetric versus globally-audited fairness) has both sides' measured overhead.

title: BAR Fault Tolerance for Cooperative Services
authors: Amitanand S. Aiyer, Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Mike Dahlin, Jean-Philippe Martin, Carl Porth
why_needed: Defines the Byzantine-Altruistic-Rational participant model, in which a protocol must be simultaneously safe against Byzantine participants and incentive-compatible against rational ones that deviate only when deviation is individually profitable, and gives a cooperative backup service built to that combined guarantee; needed because every incentive mechanism selected in this domain must be checked against this three-way model rather than against a Byzantine-only or rational-only threat model, which is a composition question the brief's cross-component conflict check is built to catch.

title: A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays
authors: Mainak Ghosh, Miles Richardson, Bryan Ford, Rob Jansen
venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs)
why_needed: TorPath forms Tor circuits so that circuit participants can jointly measure end-to-end goodput on that specific circuit and collectively mine a currency unit (TorCoin) in proportion to the measured goodput, without a central bandwidth authority; this is the direct answer this domain must extract for whether goodput on a specific path, rather than a self-report, can back an incentive currency, and at what verification cost.

title: From Onions to Shallots: Rewarding Tor Relays with TEARS
authors: Rob Jansen, Andrew Miller, Paul Syverson, Bryan Ford
venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs)
why_needed: A second bandwidth-reward currency proposed at the same workshop as TorCoin, using a trusted-directory-signed measurement rather than TorCoin's peer-measured circuit goodput; needed as the direct trust-model comparison point (trusted measurement authority versus peer measurement) for verifiable bandwidth accounting, one of the brief's named open problems for this domain.

title: Proof-of-Work as Anonymous Micropayment: Rewarding a Tor Relay
authors: Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov
why_needed: A third relay-reward construction using client-side proof-of-work as the unit of payment instead of a measured-bandwidth currency, removing the need for any bandwidth measurement at all; needed to check whether replacing bandwidth verification with computational proof of work changes the security assumption from third-party bandwidth measurement to third-party-verifiable computation, and at what stated cost to the client.

title: PeerFlow: Secure Load Balancing in Tor
authors: Aaron Johnson, Rob Jansen, Nicholas Hopper, Aaron Segal, Paul Syverson
why_needed: Shows that Tor's existing bandwidth-authority measurement (TorFlow) can be manipulated by a relay to gain disproportionate traffic share, gives the measured gain from the manipulation, and proposes a peer-measurement replacement bounded against that manipulation; needed as the direct evidence that a bandwidth-ordered or bandwidth-rewarded overlay's self-reported or centrally measured bandwidth is an attack surface, which is exactly HSkip+'s undefended honest-reporting assumption noted as an open problem in this project's brief.

title: FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor
authors: Matthew Traudt, Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson
why_needed: Replaces the passive, slow-to-converge bandwidth measurement PeerFlow and TorFlow rely on with an active, adaptively-scheduled load test that a relay cannot inflate without also carrying the traffic, stating a measured convergence-time improvement over the prior measurement system; needed as the most recent (2021) advance in third-party bandwidth verification, checked against the 2024 result below for whether it has itself since been superseded.

title: Proof of Backhaul: Trustfree Measurement of Broadband Bandwidth
authors: Peiyao Sheng, Nikita Yadav, Vishal Sevani, Arun Babu, S. V. R. Anand, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath
why_needed: A 2024 construction for a client to prove its own broadband backhaul bandwidth to a remote verifier without a trusted local measurement device, targeted directly at the brief's named open question of whether cheap third-party bandwidth verification exists; needed to determine whether this is a general answer to that question or specific to a broadband-access setting that does not transfer to a peer-to-peer overlay link.

title: On the Accuracy of Tor Bandwidth Estimation
authors: Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson
why_needed: An independent measurement of how accurately the deployed Tor bandwidth-measurement pipeline estimates the true capacity of a relay, using ground-truth data unavailable to the measurement system itself; this is the direct measured answer to the honest-reporting and verification-accuracy question the brief lists as open for capacity-ordered overlays, separate from any of the currency or reward-scheme proposals.

title: Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
authors: Alex Davidson, Ian Goldberg, Nick Sullivan, George Tankersley, Filippo Valsorda
why_needed: The deployed anonymous-rate-limiting-token construction the brief names directly: a client redeems one unlinkable, cryptographically blind-signed token per rate-limited action, obtained in a batch after passing one challenge, so the verifier can enforce a rate limit without learning which of a client's past challenge-passes corresponds to which later redemption; needed for its stated token-generation and redemption cost and its stated threat model limits (a verifier colluding with the issuer, or a client that shares tokens, are both out of scope as stated).

title: Round-Optimal Password-Protected Secret Sharing and T-PAKE in the Password-Only Model
authors: Stanislaw Jarecki, Aggelos Kiayias, Hugo Krawczyk
why_needed: Defines the 2HashDH oblivious pseudorandom function construction later used as the cryptographic core of Privacy Pass's token issuance: the issuer computes a keyed function of a client-blinded input without learning the input, and the client unblinds the result into an unlinkable token; needed as the underlying primitive so the security assumption Privacy Pass rests on (discrete-log hardness of the issuer's key, one-more-unforgeability of the resulting function) is traceable to its proof rather than asserted secondhand.

title: The Pythia PRF Service
authors: Adam Everspaugh, Rahul Chatterjee, Samuel Scott, Ari Juels, Thomas Ristenpart
why_needed: Deploys an oblivious pseudorandom function as a standalone rate-limiting network service: each client request is evaluated exactly once against a per-client counter enforced by the service, with the service unable to learn the client's input, and reports the achieved evaluation throughput and per-request latency; needed as the measured system-level cost of running an OPRF as a rate-limiting service rather than only as the cryptographic primitive inside a client protocol.

title: A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications
authors: Nirvan Tyagi, Sofía Celi, Thomas Ristenpart, Nick Sullivan, Stefano Tessaro, Christopher A. Wood
why_needed: Introduces the partially oblivious PRF (public metadata visible to both parties, private input still hidden) later standardized as the verifiable OPRF used in Privacy Pass's second protocol version, and states the measured evaluation-time improvement over the prior non-partially-oblivious construction it replaces; needed to determine what capability (per-issuer public metadata, meaning distinct rate-limit categories from a single key) the current deployed token scheme has that the original 2018 Privacy Pass construction lacked.

title: Anonymous Tokens with Public Metadata and Applications to Private Contact Tracing
authors: Ben Kreuter, Tancrède Lepoint, Michele Orrù, Mariana Raykova
why_needed: A second, algebraic-MAC-based construction for a rate-limiting token that carries public metadata (a rate-limit category or trust tier visible on redemption), deployed in a production contact-tracing risk-score system; needed as the direct construction-family comparison against Tyagi et al.'s partially oblivious PRF approach for the same public-metadata capability, with each side's stated computational cost.

title: Anonymous Counting Tokens
authors: Fabrice Benhamouda, Mariana Raykova, Karn Seth
why_needed: Generalizes anonymous rate-limiting tokens from a per-client global counter to a per-client-per-message counter, so an issuer can enforce that a client obtains at most one token for each distinct message while remaining unable to link a client's tokens across different messages; gives four constructions with stated tradeoffs and hardness assumptions (including one under q-DDHI and DCR). This is the 2023 advance the brief's retrieval instructions flag as necessary to check against any older, coarser-grained token scheme selected for this domain.

title: WAKU-RLN-RELAY: Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Economic Spam Protection
authors: Sanaz Taheri-Boshrooyeh, Oskar Thorén, Barry Whitehat, Wei Jie Koh, Onur Kilic, Kobi Gurkan
why_needed: The direct academic treatment of the rate-limiting nullifier the brief names: each message carries a zero-knowledge proof of membership in a staked-deposit set plus a per-epoch nullifier derived from the sender's secret, so a second message in the same epoch reveals a linkable nullifier collision that lets any observer extract the sender's secret and forfeit its stake, without the honest sender's identity ever appearing on the wire; needed as the mechanism a client-side gossip network can use to rate-limit without any central issuer, at the stated cost of a staked deposit and a zero-knowledge proof per message.

title: Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers
authors: Alvaro Revuelta, Sergei Tikhomirov, Aaryamann Challani, Hanno Cornelius, Simon Pierre Vivier
why_needed: Measures the message-propagation latency added by attaching a rate-limiting-nullifier proof to every gossiped message in a deployed gossip-based relay network, using an analytical model, a single-host simulation at a stated node count, and a real multi-host deployment across stated geographic locations; this is the 2024 deployed-cost figure for the rate-limiting-nullifier mechanism the brief lists as an open area, needed with its exact node counts and topology rather than a rounded restatement.

title: Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions
authors: Colin Percival
venue: BSDCan (self-published technical report; later standardized as RFC 7914)
why_needed: Defines scrypt, a key-derivation function whose evaluation cost is dominated by filling and repeatedly re-reading a large pseudorandom array held in memory, so that building custom hardware to lower the per-evaluation time gains far less than it does against a purely computational function; the foundational memory-hard function the brief names, needed for its stated area-time tradeoff argument and its parameterization (memory size N, block size r, parallelization p).

title: Argon2: New Generation of Memory-Hard Functions for Password Hashing and Other Applications
authors: Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, Dmitry Khovratovich
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)
why_needed: The winner of the Password Hashing Competition, giving two variants (data-dependent Argon2d and data-independent Argon2i) with a stated time-memory tradeoff resistance proof for each and measured throughput at stated memory and pass-count parameters; needed as the current reference memory-hard construction that any rate-limiting-without-identity design in this domain would use in place of the older scrypt, and for the specific tradeoff (Argon2d resists tradeoff attacks better but leaks memory-access patterns; Argon2i does not) that decides which variant a given threat model requires.

title: Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing
authors: Joël Alwen, Jeremiah Blocki
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)
why_needed: Gives a computed depth-reduction attack against the data-independent memory-hard functions (Argon2i, Balloon Hashing) at their standardized pass-count parameters, stating the achieved reduction in effective memory-hardness at those parameters; needed as the direct critique bounding how many passes a data-independent memory-hard function needs before its data-independence stops paying for the side-channel resistance it is chosen for.

title: Balloon Hashing: A Memory-Hard Function Providing Provable Protection Against Sequential Attacks
authors: Dan Boneh, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Stuart Schechter
why_needed: A data-independent memory-hard function with a stated formal proof of memory-hardness against a sequential (non-parallel) evaluator, offered as a licensing-unencumbered alternative to Argon2 with a different construction (a stack of expander-graph-connected buffers rather than Argon2's data-dependent shuffling); needed as the construction Alwen and Blocki's 2017 attack above is stated against, so the attack's target and the construction's proof can be checked against each other directly.

title: Client Puzzles: A Cryptographic Countermeasure Against Connection Depletion Attacks
authors: Ari Juels, John Brainard
why_needed: Defines an interactive challenge-response puzzle a server issues before committing a scarce resource to a connection request, with a stated property that the puzzle's difficulty can be scaled by the server in response to observed load without changing the protocol; needed as the interactive-puzzle branch of rate-limiting-without-identity, distinct from HashCash's non-interactive self-generated stamp, with its own cost and its own failure condition (a server under attack must still generate and track outstanding puzzles).

title: Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail
authors: Cynthia Dwork, Moni Naor
why_needed: The originating paper for the idea underlying every proof-of-work rate limiter in this domain: a sender attaches to each request a value expensive to compute but cheap for the receiver to check, so the receiver can require one per request without maintaining any per-sender state or identity; needed to determine what the original paper actually proves about the cost gap between computing and checking, since HashCash and every rate-limiting proof-of-work scheme in this domain traces its security argument back to this construction.

title: Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
authors: Adam Back
why_needed: The specific non-interactive proof-of-work stamp construction (a partial hash-collision search over a string carrying the resource, a timestamp, and a nonce) used as the HashCash rate limiter named directly in the brief, and reused inside the 4P protocol already in this project's evidence file as a per-request rate limiter against private-set-intersection enumeration; needed for its stated verification cost (one hash) against its stated generation cost (an expected number of hash attempts set by a leading-zero-bit count) so that cost ratio can be checked against later VDF-based alternatives.

title: Verifiable Delay Functions
authors: Dan Boneh, Joseph Bonneau, Benedikt Bünz, Ben Fisch
why_needed: Defines a verifiable delay function: a computation that takes a stated minimum number of sequential steps even on unbounded parallel hardware, produces a unique output for a given input, and comes with a proof checkable far faster than the computation itself; unlike a memory-hard function or ordinary proof-of-work, a VDF's minimum-time property does not degrade under parallel or ASIC hardware, which the paper states directly and proves under a sequentiality conjecture on repeated squaring in a group of unknown order. Needed as the foundational primitive for rate limiting by elapsed real time rather than by consumed computation or memory, with its stated construction cost and its stated open problem (a plausible sequentiality assumption without a reduction to a standard hardness problem).

title: Simple Verifiable Delay Functions
authors: Krzysztof Pietrzak
why_needed: An independent, concurrently developed verifiable delay function construction over the same repeated-squaring-in-an-unknown-order-group setting as Boneh, Bonneau, Bünz, and Fisch, with a different, interactive-turned-non-interactive proof of correctness; needed as the direct construction-level comparison (proof size, verifier computation) against the other 2018/2019 VDF constructions in this domain, since VDF deployments (Chia, Ethereum research) had to choose between this and Wesolowski's construction below on stated grounds.

title: Efficient Verifiable Delay Functions
authors: Benjamin Wesolowski
why_needed: A third repeated-squaring-based verifiable delay function construction with a stated constant-size proof and stated constant verifier time independent of the delay parameter, the two properties on which it is preferred over Pietrzak's construction in deployed systems; needed with its exact stated proof size and verification cost so the tradeoff against Pietrzak's larger but simpler-to-generate proof is a cited comparison rather than an assumed one.

title: Studying the Workload of a Fully Decentralized Web3 System: IPFS
authors: Pedro Ákos Costa, João Leitão, Yiannis Psaras
why_needed: Independent workload characterization of IPFS content-identifier retrieval and location-record lookup at multi-million-CID scale; the prior pass cited an average and a maximum retrieval-latency figure from this paper's arXiv preprint without opening it, so the full text must be checked against that carried-forward number before it is used again.

title: Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case
authors: Aravindh Raman, Sagar Joglekar, Emiliano De Cristofaro, Nishanth Sastry, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: Founding measurement of Mastodon/ActivityPub federation concentration, including the simulated-outage figures (largest-connected-component collapse from removing autonomous systems, post share removed by instance outages) that quantify re-concentration with numbers rather than narrative, directly answering the domain's causal-evidence request.

title: Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon
authors: Lucio La Cava, Sergio Greco, Andrea Tagarelli
why_needed: Post-2019 growth and instance-concentration measurement of the fediverse, needed to determine whether Raman et al.'s 2019 concentration figures held, worsened, or improved as the network grew, which the domain brief singles out as the highest-value kind of finding.

title: An evidence-based and critical analysis of the Fediverse decentralization promises
authors: Henrique S. Xavier
why_needed: A named critique testing the fediverse's decentralization claims against measured data; not confirmed in a peer-reviewed venue on DBLP, so its figures need a full-text pass to separate its measurements from its argument before either enters the evidence file.

title: A Herd of Young Mastodonts: the User-Centered Footprints of Newcomers After Twitter Acquisition
authors: Francesco Di Cursi, Chiara Boldrini, Andrea Passarella, Marco Conti
venue: IEEE International Conference on Big Data
why_needed: Measures where a large wave of new users actually settled inside the fediverse's instance topology after a centralized-platform exit event, the direct empirical case of whether an open migration path redistributes users or reconcentrates them onto a few instances.

title: Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media
authors: Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jake Gold, Jay Graber, Daniel Holmgren, Devin Ivy, Jeromy Johnson, Bryan Newbold, Jaz Volpert
why_needed: The architecture paper for the AT Protocol (account portability, separated hosting/relay/AppView roles, decentralized identifiers), written by the protocol's own designers; every Bluesky concentration measurement compares actual deployment against this design's stated separation of components.

title: Looking AT the Blue Skies of Bluesky
authors: Leonhard Balduf, Saidu Sokoto, Onur Ascigil, Gareth Tyson, Björn Scheuermann, Maciej Korczynski, Ignacio Castro, Michal Król
why_needed: The first large-scale measurement of Bluesky's decomposed architecture, collecting data across every AT Protocol subcomponent (personal data servers, relays, AppViews, labelers) and assessing provider diversity for each; this is the direct 2024 test of whether decomposing a platform into swappable subcomponents actually produces provider diversity or re-concentrates each subcomponent separately.

title: The Rise of Bluesky
authors: Ozgur Can Seckin, Filipi Nascimento Silva, Bao Tran Truong, Sangyeon Kim, Fan Huang, Alessandro Flammini, Filippo Menczer
why_needed: Growth-phase measurement of Bluesky's user base and network structure following its public opening, the temporal complement to Balduf et al.'s architectural snapshot; needed to state whether the measured provider concentration changed as the user count grew by orders of magnitude.

title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
authors: Yiluo Wei, Gareth Tyson
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Networking
why_needed: Direct measurement of relay-level concentration in Nostr and the bandwidth/storage overhead of replicating every followed identity's log to every relay a user connects to; the load-bearing source for any Nostr relay-diversity or replication-cost claim in this domain.

title: Understanding User-Generated Content and Communities in Decentralized Web3 Networks: An Empirical Study on Nostr
authors: Shutong Qu, Chunyang Li, Hongzhou Chen, Wei Cai
venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications (TOMCCAP)
why_needed: A second, independent 2026 empirical measurement of Nostr content and community structure, needed to check Wei and Tyson's relay-concentration and availability figures against a differently constructed dataset before either is treated as settled.

title: Crawling BitTorrent DHTs for Fun and Profit
authors: Scott Wolchok, J. Alex Halderman
why_needed: Demonstrates that the BitTorrent mainline DHT (distinct from Kad) can be crawled to reconstruct which peers are downloading which content at scale, an operational-privacy failure of a widely deployed unmodified DHT that any content-location design in this architecture must either avoid or account for.

title: Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT
authors: Liang Wang, Jussi Kangasharju
why_needed: Measures identity-forgery attacks actually observed in the live BitTorrent mainline DHT rather than injected experimentally, giving a real-deployment base rate for Sybil presence in a DHT with no admission control, the empirical counterpart the domain brief asks for alongside narrative claims.

title: Gossiping with Append-Only Logs in Secure-Scuttlebutt
authors: Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Erick Lavoie, Christian F. Tschudin
why_needed: Measures the per-connection request overhead and message-propagation cost of Secure Scuttlebutt's gossip replication protocol, the specific figures needed to state what a full sync of a new identity actually costs, which the prior pass described only in narrative terms (large initial-sync volume, no measured figure).

title: A Glimpse of the Matrix: Scalability Issues of a New Message-Oriented Data Synchronization Middleware
authors: Florian Jacob, Jan Grashöfer, Hannes Hartenstein
venue: ACM Middleware Demos/Posters (extended version on arXiv)
why_needed: First independent measurement of the deployed public Matrix federation's scaling behavior, needed for the per-room server-resource-consumption figures the domain brief asks for; the prior pass described Matrix's cost only as 'computationally complex' with no cited number.

title: Matrix Decomposition: Analysis of an Access Control Approach on Transaction-based DAGs without Finality
authors: Florian Jacob, Luca Becker, Jan Grashöfer, Hannes Hartenstein
why_needed: Independent formal analysis of Matrix's State Resolution v2 access-control algorithm (the mechanism that makes per-room state resolution computationally expensive), stating what guarantees it does and does not provide; needed to trace the specific mechanism behind the resource-consumption figures in Jacob et al.'s 2019 measurement.

title: Matrix Protocol: A Comprehensive Systematic Mapping Study
authors: José A. P. Martins, Paulo A. L. Rego, José A. F. de Macêdo, Francisco Airton Silva, Vinícius Lagrota
why_needed: 2026 systematic mapping of published Matrix-protocol research, satisfying the domain's requirement for a current survey and providing a bibliography of every scaling and resource-consumption study to check this target list against for completeness.

title: Measuring Freenet in the Wild: Censorship-Resilience under Observation
authors: Stefanie Roos, Benjamin Schiller, Stefan Hacker, Thorsten Strufe
why_needed: Active-monitoring measurement of the deployed Freenet (now Hyphanet) network's concurrent node count and per-node session-length/inter-session-length churn distribution, and of how far an observer can track individual node online-time from outside; the operational-measurement counterpart to the Pitch Black attack paper already read in full, needed to separate Freenet's ordinary churn-driven degradation from its adversarial degradation.

title: Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization
authors: Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov, Ralf-Philipp Weinmann
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
why_needed: Measures how much of the Tor hidden-service address space could be enumerated and deanonymized using a cheap Sybil attack against the hidden-service directory, the concrete cost/exposure figures needed to evaluate any Tor-based rendezvous mechanism this architecture might reuse for reachability behind NAT.

title: Users Get Routed: Traffic Correlation on Tor by Realistic Adversaries
authors: Aaron Johnson, Chris Wacek, Rob Jansen, Micah Sherr, Paul F. Syverson
why_needed: States measured circuit-compromise probabilities for realistic autonomous-system-level and relay-operator-level adversaries against deployed Tor, as a function of user behavior and time online; the concrete cost figures behind the onion-routing tier's stated adversary model, which the prior pass summarized only as 'over 500ms delay' with no compromise-probability figure.

title: RAPTOR: Routing Attacks on Privacy in Tor
authors: Yixin Sun, Anne Edmundson, Laurent Vanbever, Oscar Li, Jennifer Rexford, Mung Chiang, Prateek Mittal
why_needed: Shows that a network-level (BGP/AS-path) adversary can deanonymize Tor users by manipulating routing itself rather than by running Tor relays, measured against the live Tor network topology; needed because it bounds Tor's anonymity guarantee by an adversary class outside the relay-operator threat model the other Tor measurement papers in this list assume.

title: Changing of the Guards: A Framework for Understanding and Improving Entry Guard Selection in Tor
authors: Tariq Elahi, Kevin S. Bauer, Mashael AlSabah, Roger Dingledine, Ian Goldberg
why_needed: Measures how concentrated the deployed Tor network's entry-guard selection is around a small set of high-bandwidth relays, and the resulting exposure to a guard-operating adversary; the direct guard-concentration figure for any capacity-ordered or bandwidth-weighted relay-selection mechanism this architecture might adopt for its own privacy tiers.

title: Measuring Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum using Multiple Metrics and Granularities
authors: Qinwei Lin, Chao Li, Xifeng Zhao, Xianhai Chen
why_needed: Foundational multi-metric measurement of mining/validation concentration in both Bitcoin and Ethereum at multiple granularities (address, entity, geography), the baseline every later single-metric Ethereum client-diversity or RPC-concentration measurement narrows down from.

title: Unveiling Ethereum's P2P Network: The Role of Chain and Client Diversity
authors: Jiahao Luo
why_needed: Direct 2025 measurement of client-implementation and peer-to-peer network diversity in deployed Ethereum, the specific node-distribution concentration figure named in the domain brief; not yet in a peer-reviewed venue on DBLP, so the full-text pass must confirm its measurement method before any figure is carried forward.

title: SoK: Measuring Blockchain Decentralization
authors: Christina Ovezik, Dimitris Karakostas, Mary Milad, Daniel W. Woods, Aggelos Kiayias
why_needed: 2025 Systematization of Knowledge over every published blockchain-decentralization metric, the survey the domain brief asks for and the source most likely to state whether an academic measurement of RPC-provider concentration (as opposed to mining/validator concentration) exists at all.

title: SoK: A Stratified Approach to Blockchain Decentralization
authors: Christina Ovezik, Dimitris Karakostas, Aggelos Kiayias
why_needed: Earlier, 2024 SoK by the same lead authors proposing the layered (network/consensus/application) decomposition that the 2025 ACNS SoK above builds on; needed to trace which decentralization metrics are original to which paper before citing either.

title: Neither Snow Nor Rain Nor MITM...: An Empirical Analysis of Email Delivery Security
authors: Zakir Durumeric, David Adrian, Ariana Mirian, James Kasten, Elie Bursztein, Nicolas Lidzborski, Kurt Thomas, Vijay Eranti, Michael D. Bailey, J. Alex Halderman
why_needed: Measures SMTP transport-security deployment across the Alexa top million domains' mail infrastructure and across live Gmail-observed inbound/outbound traffic; the closest available primary measurement of email-provider concentration found in this pass (no dedicated academic market-concentration study for email surfaced under any search phrasing tried) and must be read to determine whether it separately reports provider-level traffic share or only security-protocol adoption.

title: Bluesky: Network topology, polarization, and algorithmic curation
authors: Dorian Quelle, Alexandre Bovet
why_needed: Reports that of roughly 5 million measured Bluesky accounts, about 139,000 (approximately 2.8%) had liked at least one non-default feed, i.e. had ever engaged with an alternative to the platform-supplied default. This is the direct measured answer the domain brief asks for on what fraction of users actually change a default ranking setting, which decides whether client-selected ranking changes real user exposure or stays a capability nobody exercises.

title: Whose Posts Get Ranked: Identical-Text Exposure Gaps in Bluesky Custom Feeds
authors: Yipeng Wang, Mohit Singhal
why_needed: Repeatedly snapshots the Top-50 lists of 1,366 public Bluesky custom feeds and finds that for identical post text, one copy appears on a feed's ranked list while another copy does not in roughly a third of cases, correlated with the posting account's prior history on that specific feed. This is a measured failure condition of client-selected, third-party ranking: two mechanically identical inputs receive different exposure, which any ranking-without-a-global-index selection must account for.

title: Understanding Decentralized Social Feed Curation on Mastodon
authors: Yuhan Liu, Emmy Song, Owen Xingjian Zhang, Jewel Merriman, Lei Zhang, Andrés Monroy-Hernández
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
why_needed: Studies how Mastodon users construct and share feed-curation practices (lists, hashtag following, third-party tools) in the absence of any platform-supplied ranking algorithm, i.e. the reverse-chronological-only baseline against which Bluesky's feed-generator marketplace is a contrast. Needed to establish what unranked, no-global-index feed consumption looks like in a deployed system of comparable scale.

title: Flocking to Mastodon: Tracking the Great Twitter Migration
authors: Jiahui He, Haris Bin Zia, Ignacio Castro, Aravindh Raman, Nishanth Sastry, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: Measures the 2022 Twitter-to-Mastodon migration cohort at scale: which instances absorbed the new accounts, how quickly newcomers left again, and how instance choice concentrated. Supplies measured churn and concentration numbers for a real onboarding event onto a federated system, which any decentralized-web client claiming to reproduce mainstream-platform usage patterns needs as a baseline for what happens when a large cohort arrives at once.

title: An Exploration of Decentralized Moderation on Mastodon
authors: Carlo Alberto Bono, Lucio La Cava, Luca Luceri, Francesco Pierri
why_needed: Measures moderation actions (suspensions, silences, defederations) actually issued by Mastodon instance administrators and characterizes which instances issue them, at what rate, and against which targets. Supplies the measured baseline for instance-level, admin-issued moderation that a composable-labeler design is proposed as a replacement for.

title: Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse
authors: Ishaku Hassan Anaobi, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Haris Bin Zia, Damilola Ibosiola, Gareth Tyson
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW)
why_needed: Measures the moderation workload carried by individual Mastodon instance administrators as the fediverse grew after the 2022 Twitter migration, quantifying reports handled per admin and the tooling gaps admins report. This is the measured cost side of instance-operator-driven moderation, needed to compare against the operating cost of composable labeler services run by dedicated parties.

title: Self-moderation in the Decentralized Era: Decoding Blocking Behavior on Bluesky
authors: Carlo Bono, Nick Liu, Giuseppe Russo, Francesco Pierri
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
why_needed: Measures individual-account blocking on Bluesky at scale: who blocks whom, how block relationships cluster, and how blocking functions as a per-user moderation signal distinct from both instance-level defederation and labeler subscription. Needed as the measured behavior of the third moderation primitive (individual user block lists) alongside instance blocking and composable labelers.

title: "A Blocklist is a Boundary": Tensions between Community Protection and Mutual Aid on Federated Social Networks
authors: Erika Melder, Ada Lerner, Michael Ann DeVito
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI)
why_needed: Interview-based study of fediverse blocklist curators, server operators, and affected users that identifies the specific failure condition of shared community-level blocklists: federation encodes default-on interaction and instance-level block decisions cut off users who had no part in making them, severing mutual-aid ties. Supplies the measured (interview-derived) failure mode of shared block lists as a fact distinct from any judgment about whether to use them.

title: Understanding Community-Level Blocklists in Decentralized Social Media
authors: Owen Xingjian Zhang, Sohyeon Hwang, Yuhan Liu, Manoel Horta Ribeiro, Andrés Monroy-Hernández
why_needed: Measures how shared instance blocklists propagate and get adopted across Mastodon instances, and quantifies how much of the network a given blocklist's adoption actually isolates. Supplies the measured reach and adoption pattern of the shared-blocklist mechanism, complementing the qualitative failure modes in Melder et al.

title: Collaborative Content Moderation in the Fediverse
authors: Haris Bin Zia, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Gareth Tyson
why_needed: Proposes and evaluates a moderation architecture in which instances share moderation signals (not final decisions) with each other rather than each instance moderating in isolation or defederating wholesale. A competing point in the moderation-architecture design space against both Bluesky-style composable labelers and Mastodon-style unilateral instance blocking, with its own measured tradeoffs.

title: On the Effects of Decentralized Moderation on Network Robustness and Information Diffusion in Mastodon
authors: Beatriz Arregui-García, Lucio La Cava, Anees Baqir, Andrea Tagarelli, Riccardo Gallotti, Sandro Meloni
why_needed: Measures how instance-level defederation changes the connectivity and information-flow properties of the fediverse graph, i.e. the structural consequence of decentralized moderation decisions on the network as a whole rather than only on the instance that issues them. Needed to check whether moderation decisions made locally by one instance operator degrade reachability for accounts on unrelated instances.

title: Trouble in Paradise? Understanding Mastodon Admin's Motivations, Experiences, and Challenges Running Decentralised Social Media
authors: Zhilin Zhang, Jun Zhao, Ge Wang, Samantha-Kaye Johnston, George Chalhoub, Tala Ross, Diyi Liu, Claudine Tinsman, Rui Zhao, Max Van Kleek, Nigel Shadbolt
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
why_needed: Interviews 16 Mastodon instance administrators on why they run an instance, what moderation and infrastructure work that requires, and where they say the software gives them no adequate tooling. Supplies the measured (interview-derived) operating cost of being a moderation-and-hosting operator under the instance model, which any design replacing instance operators with a different moderation locus must match or beat.

title: Understanding and Improving Content Moderation in Web3 Platforms
authors: Wenrui Zuo, Raul J. Mondragón, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
why_needed: Measures user-driven moderation on the blockchain-based microblogging platform memo.cash from 391,000 posts, and finds platform action count (not content features like hate speech) is the strongest predictor of a post being hidden, with the follower graph controlling visibility. This is a measured moderation-signal population from a platform with no instance operators at all, a data point the fediverse-only moderation literature does not cover.

title: Decentralised Moderation for Interoperable Social Networks: A Conversation-Based Approach for Pleroma and the Fediverse
authors: Vibhor Agarwal, Aravindh Raman, Nishanth Sastry, Ahmed M. Abdelmoniem, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
why_needed: Proposes moderating at the level of a conversation thread rather than a whole instance or a whole account, evaluated on Pleroma fediverse data, as a finer-grained alternative to both instance defederation and account-level blocking. A third competing point in the moderation-granularity design space, with its own measured precision/recall against the other two.

title: Decentralized Recommendation Based on Matrix Factorization: A Comparison of Gossip and Federated Learning
authors: István Hegedűs, Gábor Danner, Márk Jelasity
venue: ECML PKDD Workshops (Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases)
why_needed: Implements matrix-factorization collaborative filtering under two decentralized training regimes — gossip learning, in which a model random-walks between peers and each peer updates it with its own local ratings, versus federated learning, in which a coordinating server aggregates peer-computed updates — on the same recommendation task, and measures convergence speed and accuracy of each against each other and against a centralized baseline. Directly supplies the comparison the domain needs between the two leading decentralized-recommendation training architectures.

title: A peer-to-peer recommender system for self-emerging user communities based on gossip overlays
authors: Ranieri Baraglia, Patrizio Dazzi, Matteo Mordacchini, Laura Ricci
venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences
why_needed: Defines a recommender architecture (PREGO/T-Man derived) in which each peer maintains a gossip overlay linking it to peers with similar interest profiles, discovered purely from repeated pairwise gossip exchange with no server-side index or global item catalogue, and item recommendations are then drawn from a peer's overlay neighborhood. This is a foundational, fully peer-to-peer (not client/server-federated) construction for the class of mechanisms the domain must cover, distinct from and earlier than the gossip-vs-federated comparison in Hegedűs et al.

title: G-Rank: Unsupervised Continuous Learn-to-Rank for Edge Devices in a P2P Network
authors: Andrew Gold, Johan Pouwelse
why_needed: Defines a ranking method that runs entirely on each requesting peer's own device, using only signals available locally (the peer's own click and dwell behavior) plus content received from other peers, with no shared training data, no central model, and no query sent to any index-holding party. This is the direct foundational mechanism for 'ranking without a global index' the domain brief names as underexplored, from the same research group (TU Delft/Tribler) responsible for the already-verified 4P search system.

title: CoolStreaming/DONet: A Data-Driven Overlay Network for Peer-to-Peer Live Media Streaming
authors: Xinyan Zhang, Jiangchuan Liu, Bo Li, Tak-Shing Peter Yum
why_needed: Defines DONet, a mesh-based (not tree-based) live-streaming overlay in which every peer periodically exchanges a data-availability map with a randomly chosen subset of partners and pulls missing pieces from whichever partner holds them, with no fixed relay-tree structure to rebuild on partner departure. The foundational data-driven alternative to relay-tree multicast (Narada, SplitStream) that the domain's peer-assisted-video and live-relay coverage must include, since CoolStreaming was an actually deployed system with a large historical user base.

title: A Measurement Study of a Large-Scale P2P IPTV System
authors: Xiaojun Hei, Chao Liang, Jian Liang, Yong Liu, Keith W. Ross
why_needed: Measures the deployed PPLive P2P IPTV system by crawling and packet-capturing live sessions: peer population per channel, the fraction of a peer's received video segments that actually come from other peers versus from dedicated servers, and how streaming continuity depends on the number of active neighbor peers. Supplies the measured peer-carried-load fraction the domain brief specifically asks for, from an actually deployed system rather than a testbed.

title: SplitStream: High-Bandwidth Multicast in Cooperative Environments
authors: Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Animesh Nandi, Antony Rowstron, Atul Singh
venue: ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP)
why_needed: Defines a live-streaming relay-tree construction in which the stream is striped into k stripes, each distributed over its own multicast tree built on a Pastry DHT, with trees constructed so that no single peer is an interior (forwarding) node in more than one tree. This bounds any one peer's forwarding load to at most one stripe's worth of bandwidth and survives a peer's departure by only breaking the trees where that peer was interior. The foundational interior-node-disjoint relay-tree mechanism the domain's live-streaming-relay-tree coverage must include, as the structured counterpart to CoolStreaming's unstructured mesh.

title: A Case for End System Multicast
authors: Yang-hua Chu, Sanjay G. Rao, Srinivasan Seshan, Hui Zhang
venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
why_needed: Defines Narada, in which participating end hosts (not routers) self-organize into a mesh overlay by exchanging membership and performance information, then run a distributed shortest-path computation over that mesh to derive per-source relay trees, with each host reoptimizing its mesh links as measured latency and loss to its current neighbors change. The foundational end-host-only (no router or dedicated-server support required) relay-tree construction, and the direct ancestor of the mesh-first, tree-second design pattern CoolStreaming and SplitStream both build on.

title: ISP-friendly Peer-assisted On-demand Streaming of Long Duration Content in BBC iPlayer
authors: Dmytro Karamshuk, Nishanth Sastry, Andrew Secker, Jigna Chandaria
why_needed: Measures a real BBC iPlayer deployment in which viewers of long-duration video-on-demand content forward already-downloaded segments to other nearby viewers, reporting the achieved fraction of total delivered bytes that peers carried versus what the origin/CDN served, broken out by content duration and by how the peer-assist scheduler was constrained to stay ISP-friendly (favoring same-ISP peers to avoid transit costs). One of the few measured peer-carried-load fractions from a production peer-assisted VoD deployment rather than a testbed or simulation.

title: Stealthy Peers: Understanding Security Risks of WebRTC-Based Peer-Assisted Video Streaming
authors: Siyuan Tang, Eihal Alowaisheq, Xianghang Mi, Yi Chen, XiaoFeng Wang, Yanzhi Dou
why_needed: Analyzes deployed WebRTC-based peer-assisted video-streaming services and demonstrates that a peer participating in delivery can be made to reveal the IP addresses and viewing activity of the other peers it is exchanging segments with, an exposure the WebRTC signaling and ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) candidate-exchange process was not designed to prevent. The measured attack and its exposed information are the specific fact any WebRTC-assisted-HLS selection for this domain must account for, independent of any vendor's own risk judgment.

title: WebRTC-based peer assisted framework for HTTP live streaming
authors: Midhul Varma, Hema Kumar Yarnagula, Venkatesh Tamarapalli
venue: International Conference on Communication Systems and Networks (COMSNETS)
why_needed: Implements HTTP Live Streaming segment delivery in which a browser fetches a segment from a nearby peer over a WebRTC data channel before falling back to the origin server, and reports the measured fraction of segment requests served by peers versus origin. Directly supplies the domain-requested measured result for 'WebRTC-assisted HLS,' the specific mechanism combination the brief names.

title: Measuring Decentralized Video Streaming: A Case Study of DTube
authors: Trinh Viet Doan, Tat Dat Pham, Markus Oberprieler, Vaibhav Bajpai
why_needed: Measures DTube, a video-sharing platform that stores video content on IPFS (content-addressed storage) and records metadata on a blockchain rather than serving from any operator-controlled server, quantifying retrieval latency, content availability over time, and how much retrieval actually flows peer-to-peer versus through IPFS gateway servers acting as a centralizing chokepoint. Supplies a measured, non-fediverse peer-assisted video deployment as a comparison point against PeerTube.

title: The Centralization of a Decentralized Video Platform: A First Characterization Of PeerTube
authors: Michael Polinski, Richard Jo, Kevin McAfee, Fabián E. Bustamante
why_needed: Crawls the deployed PeerTube network (federated ActivityPub video instances, each independently choosing whether to run WebRTC/HLS peer-assisted delivery) and measures that instance hosting concentrates geographically (roughly 70% of instances in Germany, the USA, and France) and that over 92% of videos are stored on exactly one instance with none of PeerTube's supported redundancy in use. Supplies the measured redundancy-adoption rate and geographic-concentration figures for a deployed federated video platform, distinct from any judgment about whether federation achieved its decentralization goal.

title: Peer-to-Peer Communication Across Network Address Translators
authors: Bryan Ford, Pyda Srisuresh, Dan Kegel
venue: USENIX Annual Technical Conference, General Track
why_needed: Original description of UDP and TCP hole punching as a mechanism: two peers behind independent NATs each send to the other's externally observed address, opening a path through their own translator without any special NAT-side support. Every later hole-punching measurement (Halkes/Pouwelse 2011, Trautwein et al. 2025-26) states its success rate against this mechanism definition.

title: STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)
authors: Jonathan Rosenberg, Joel Weinberger, Christian Huitema, Rohan Mahy
why_needed: Defines the four-way NAT behavior classification (full cone, restricted cone, port-restricted cone, symmetric) that every later prevalence measurement in this domain reports its percentages against. A symmetric NAT assigns a different external port per destination address, which is the behavior that defeats hole punching and forces relay fallback.

title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
authors: Marc Petit-Huguenin, Gonzalo Salgueiro, Jonathan Rosenberg, Dan Wing, Rohan Mahy, Philip Matthews
venue: IETF RFC 8489 (obsoletes RFC 5389, itself obsoleting RFC 3489's protocol machinery)
why_needed: Current STUN specification: the binding-request mechanism a client uses to learn its own server-reflexive (public) address and port, which every hole-punching and ICE candidate-gathering procedure depends on for its first step.

title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
authors: Tirumaleswar Reddy, Alan Johnston, Philip Matthews, Jonathan Rosenberg
why_needed: Defines the relay-fallback mechanism: a client allocates a public transport address on a third-party server and every packet to and from the peer transits that server. This is the cost baseline against which any direct-connection success rate (hole punching, DCUtR) is measured, because every failed direct attempt falls back to this.

title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
authors: Ari Keränen, Christer Holmberg, Jonathan Rosenberg
why_needed: Defines candidate gathering (host, server-reflexive via STUN, relayed via TURN), connectivity checks between every candidate pair, and the priority formula that selects among simultaneously viable paths. This is the procedure WebRTC and every browser peer connection runs to decide whether a direct path or a relay is used, and it is the object of the recent QUIC-multiplexing and lightweight-signaling proposals below.

title: UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild
authors: Gertjan P. Halkes, Johan A. Pouwelse
why_needed: Earliest large-scale in-network measurement of hole-punching success on a production P2P system (the Tribler/IPv8 network at TU Delft), predating the 2025-26 DCUtR study by 14 years. Establishes the historical baseline for what fraction of peers sit behind a NAT type that allows puncturing and what fraction of attempts between them succeed, which the newer DCUtR figures must be read against as a before/after comparison rather than in isolation.

title: Mass Adoption of NATs: Survey and experiments on carrier-grade NATs
authors: Orestis Kanaris, Johan Pouwelse
why_needed: The 2023-or-later survey this domain requires. Covers carrier-grade NAT (CGN) deployment specifically, run by the same TU Delft group as the 2011 hole-punching baseline, so it is positioned to state what changed for P2P reachability between 2011 and 2023 on the operator side rather than the client side.

title: An Untold Story of Middleboxes in Cellular Networks
authors: Zhaoguang Wang, Zhiyun Qian, Qiang Xu, Zhuoqing Morley Mao, Ming Zhang
why_needed: Direct, controlled measurement of NAT and firewall behavior across carriers, distinguishing mapping type (endpoint-independent/full-cone vs. endpoint-dependent/symmetric) from filtering type and from binding timeout, on cellular networks specifically. This is the primary source the domain's cellular-symmetric-NAT prevalence figures must be checked against rather than restated from a secondary blog summary.

title: A Multi-perspective Analysis of Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment
authors: Philipp Richter, Florian Wohlfart, Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, Mark Allman, Randy Bush, Anja Feldmann, Christian Kreibich, Nicholas Weaver, Vern Paxson
why_needed: Multi-vantage-point (traceroute, BISmark home-router, and Netalyzr client-side) measurement of how many access networks interpose carrier-grade NAT between a residential subscriber and the public Internet, i.e. how often a subscriber has no directly assignable public address at all regardless of what their own equipment does. Bounds the ceiling on end-to-end direct reachability independent of the two peers' own hole-punching behavior.

title: Inferring Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment in the Wild
authors: Ioana Livadariu, Karyn Benson, Ahmed Elmokashfi, Amogh Dhamdhere, Alberto Dainotti
why_needed: A second, methodologically distinct (large-scale active-probing rather than vantage-point-limited) measurement of carrier-grade NAT prevalence, two years after Richter et al. Needed as the comparison figure to check whether the 2016 estimate held, rose, or fell, and to check which measurement technique the numbers used in synthesis should cite as closer to a global figure.

title: Large-Scale Measurement of NAT Traversal for the Decentralized Web: A Case Study of DCUtR in IPFS
authors: Dennis Trautwein, Cornelius Ihle, Moritz Schubotz, Corinna Breitinger, Bela Gipp
venue: arXiv preprint (CoRR); DOI registered for a forthcoming ACM venue but not yet resolving as of retrieval; an earlier four-author preprint titled "Challenging Tribal Knowledge -- Large Scale Measurement Campaign on Decentralized NAT Traversal" (arXiv 2510.27500, Oct. 2025) is the same underlying study
why_needed: The measurement this domain is defined around. First large-scale, longitudinal measurement of the Direct Connection Upgrade through Relay (DCUtR) hole-punching protocol on a production libp2p network (IPFS): 4.4 million traversal attempts, 85,000+ networks, 167 countries. Reports a hole-punching-stage success rate of 70% +/- 7.1% CONDITIONAL on prerequisite relay reservation and public-address discovery already having succeeded (the published-version abstract's own wording, which corrects the unconditional framing an earlier draft implied), TCP and QUIC statistically indistinguishable at ~70%, success independent of which relay coordinated the attempt, and 97.6% of successes completing on the first attempt. The conditioning clause is load-bearing: this is not the fraction of all connection attempts that reach a direct path, only the fraction of the already-relay-connected subset that then upgrades.

title: Beware: NAT Traversal is a Simple and Efficient Approach to Open Firewall Holes
authors: Elias P. Duarte Jr., Kleber V. Cardoso, Micael O. M. C. de Mello, João G. G. Borges
why_needed: States hole punching as an exploitable primitive: an attacker who controls one endpoint of a coordinated punch can use the technique to induce a NAT or stateful firewall to accept inbound packets on a port it would otherwise drop, independent of any P2P application's own intent. This is the security exposure that a direct-reachability design has to weigh against the connectivity gain, stated as a mechanism and a failure condition rather than as a value judgment about whether to use hole punching at all.

title: The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment
authors: Adam Langley, Alistair Riddoch, Alyssa Wilk, Antonio Vicente, Charles Krasic, Dan Zhang, Fan Yang, Fedor Kouranov, Ian Swett, Janardhan Iyengar, Jeff Bailey, Jeremy Dorfman, Jim Roskind, Joanna Kulik, Patrik Westin, Raman Tenneti, Robbie Shade, Ryan Hamilton, Victor Vasiliev, Wan-Teh Chang, Zhongyi Shi
why_needed: Defines QUIC: a transport multiplexed over UDP with a 0- or 1-round-trip handshake combining transport and cryptographic setup, per-stream flow control avoiding head-of-line blocking across streams, and connection IDs that let a connection survive a change of IP address or port (a NAT rebinding, or a client moving from Wi-Fi to cellular) without a new handshake. The connection-ID-based migration mechanism is the property every later QUIC-for-NAT-traversal proposal in this domain builds on.

title: Taking a Long Look at QUIC: An Approach for Rigorous Evaluation of Rapidly Evolving Transport Protocols
authors: Arash Molavi Kakhki, Samuel Jero, David Choffnes, Cristina Nita-Rotaru, Alan Mislove
venue: ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC); journal version in Communications of the ACM, 2019
why_needed: Independent, controlled comparison of QUIC against TCP+TLS across a matrix of emulated network conditions (packet loss, latency) rather than QUIC's own designers' benchmarks. Needed as the comparison-side numbers for any claim that QUIC outperforms TCP for a peer-to-peer transport, and as a caution that a rapidly evolving protocol's measured advantage in one snapshot version may not hold in a later one, which the IMC 2024 replication below tests directly.

title: Replication: "Taking a long look at QUIC"
authors: Naveenraj Muthuraj, Nooshin Eghbal, Paul Lu
why_needed: Re-runs the Kakhki et al. 2017 QUIC-vs-TCP comparison seven years later against the now-standardized IETF QUIC (RFC 9000) rather than Google's pre-standard GQUIC. Directly tests whether the 2017 comparison still holds after the protocol changed, which is exactly the forward-mining check this domain's brief requires before any 2017 QUIC performance number is carried into a 2026 architecture.

title: Implementing NAT Hole Punching with QUIC
authors: Jinyu Liang, Wei Xu, Taotao Wang, Qing Yang, Shengli Zhang
why_needed: Proposes and measures a QUIC-based hole-punching scheme as a direct alternative to TCP-based hole punching, reporting reduced punching time in weak-network conditions, and separately measures reconnection cost after a punched path breaks (from a network transition or a NAT binding timeout): QUIC connection migration restores the path 2 round trips faster than QUIC re-punching and 3 round trips faster than TCP re-punching. This is a transport property (connection migration) avoiding repetition of the NAT-traversal procedure rather than a faster way to repeat it.

title: An Analysis of QUIC Connection Migration in the Wild
authors: Aurélien Buchet, Cristel Pelsser
why_needed: Internet-wide active scan measuring what fraction of deployed QUIC servers actually support the connection-migration mechanism the QUIC specification defines and that the NAT-traversal proposals above depend on, as opposed to what the specification permits in principle. Needed because a migration-dependent NAT-resilience design is only as good as server-side deployment of the feature, and this paper states that some of the most-visited destinations do not yet support it.

title: QUIC as Multiplexing Layer in WebRTC
authors: Mathis Engelbart, Fabian Willi Fromwald, Jörg Ott
why_needed: Proposes replacing WebRTC's separate DTLS/SCTP data-channel stack and SRTP media stack with a single QUIC connection carrying both, removing one of the two independent NAT-traversal and encryption handshakes a browser peer connection currently runs. Directly answers the domain question of what a browser tab's transport stack can be simplified to, as opposed to what it is today.

title: Lightweight Call Signaling and Peer-to-Peer Control of WebRTC Video Conferencing
authors: Kundan Singh
why_needed: Describes and implements a multiparty WebRTC application with no media server: signaling piggybacks on existing push notifications or on email, and conference control and data storage run over a peer-to-peer network of the browser clients themselves using WebRTC data channels.
