States what a set of browser tabs, with no server in the data path and only a minimal signaling channel, can be made to do as a self-organizing network.

title: rtc_peer_connection.cc: kMaxPeerConnections limit enforced by RTCPeerConnection construction
authors: Chromium project (Blink renderer, third_party/blink/renderer/modules/peerconnection)
why_needed: Primary-source (source code, read directly, not a snippet) statement of a browser tab's hard connection ceiling: the constant kMaxPeerConnections = 500 is checked at every RTCPeerConnection construction, and construction past the limit throws rather than degrading. This is a concrete, versioned bound on what a browser tab can do as a network participant, not a claim about it.

title: Circuit Relay v2 (libp2p specification)
authors: Dimitris Vyzovitis (@vyzo), with interest-group review by Max Inden, Steven Allen, Raúl Kripalani
venue: libp2p/specs repository, recommendation-stage specification, revision r3
why_needed: Defines the store-and-forward relay mechanism DCUtR (Trautwein et al., above) upgrades away from when direct connectivity succeeds: a relay accepts a bounded, time-limited, data-capped reservation from a private peer and forwards a limited-duration circuit to it, so a public peer can serve as a relay without unbounded resource exposure. This is the relay-fallback cost structure (reservation duration default, per-relay concurrent-reservation cap, per-circuit data cap) that any relay-based fallback cost figure in this domain must be stated against, replacing circuit-relay v1's unreserved, uncapped resource use.

title: Rewarding relays for decentralised NAT traversal using smart contracts
authors: Navin V. Keizer, Onur Ascigil, Ioannis Psaras, George Pavlou
venue: ACM International Symposium on Theory, Algorithmic Foundations, and Protocol Design for Mobile Networks and Mobile Computing (MobiHoc)
why_needed: Addresses relay-fallback cost from the supplier side: relaying every packet for a symmetric-NAT peer consumes the relay operator's own bandwidth with no protocol-level return, so this paper measures a smart-contract-mediated payment mechanism intended to recruit relay capacity. Extract the measured relay bandwidth cost and the participation-rate effect of the reward mechanism as fact; the payment design itself is one candidate mechanism among others for solving the same supply problem, not a settled requirement.

title: POST: A Secure, Resilient, Cooperative Messaging System
authors: Alan Mislove, Ansley Post, Charles Reis, Paul Willmann, Peter Druschel, Dan S. Wallach, Xavier Bonnaire, Pierre Sens, Jean-Michel Busca, Luciana Bezerra Arantes
venue: USENIX Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS)
why_needed: Store-and-forward relay design for a recipient who is not currently reachable: each user's messages are stored redundantly across a set of nodes selected by a structured overlay (Pastry) rather than at a single mailbox server, and delivery to an offline recipient completes when that recipient's client next contacts any node holding a replica. This is the foundational design point for store-and-forward relaying in a decentralized setting, predating and structurally distinct from the mobile-push-plus-central-relay pattern used by today's platform-dependent messaging apps.

title: Measuring IPv6 Adoption
authors: Jakub Czyz, Mark Allman, Jing Zhang, Scott Iekel-Johnson, Eric Osterweil, Michael Bailey
why_needed: Multi-vantage-point (traffic, routing, DNS, active-probing) measurement establishing the earlier baseline of global IPv6 adoption that the 2025-26 measurements below report growth against. Needed for a before/after comparison rather than treating a single recent number as if adoption had always been at that level.

title: Measuring the Deployment of IPv6: Topology, Routing and Performance
authors: Amogh Dhamdhere, Matthew Luckie, Bradley Huffaker, kc claffy, Ahmed Elmokashfi, Emile Aben
why_needed: Earlier still IPv6 deployment measurement, covering AS-level topology and routing in addition to adoption share, giving a three-point (2012, 2014, 2025-26) trend for how directly reachable a dual-stack or IPv6-only peer has become over the period this domain must design for.

title: Measuring NAT64 Usage in the Wild
authors: Elizabeth Boswell, Stephen McQuistin, Colin Perkins, Stephen Strowes
why_needed: NAT64 translates between an IPv6-only client network and IPv4-only destinations, which is a second, structurally different address-translation layer from consumer/carrier-grade NAT44 and imposes its own reachability constraint on a peer trying to be dialable: an IPv6-only host behind NAT64 cannot receive an unsolicited inbound connection from an IPv4-only peer at all without a translator-side mapping. States how widely NAT64 is deployed and under what conditions, which any IPv6-first reachability design has to account for as a still-present, not disappearing, translation boundary.

title: Revisiting and Expanding the IPv6 Network Periphery: Global-Scale Measurement and Security Analysis
authors: Zixuan Xie, Zitao Yang, Shurui Fang, Zhaoyang Li, Wenxing Xie, Nannan Fu, Liangyu Dong, Xiang Li
why_needed: Global-scale active scan (73 countries/regions) identifying over 281.9 million active IPv6 network-periphery devices, a direct measurement of how many end-host addresses are live and probeable at the network edge rather than merely how many prefixes are routed. This is the device-level reachability count the domain's IPv6-direct-connectivity claims need, as distinct from AS-level or prefix-level adoption statistics.

title: Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption
authors: Sulyab Thottungal Valapu, John Heidemann
why_needed: Argues and measures that IPv6 capability is not a single yes/no property per user or service: client-side IPv6 traffic share varies with a standard deviation over 15% across users and across days for the same user, and only 12.6% of the top 100,000 websites are fully IPv6-ready end to end (as opposed to partially, through IPv4-only dependencies). A design that assumes 'the client has IPv6' or 'the destination has IPv6' as a fixed property, rather than a fluctuating one, is checked against this paper's own measured variance.

title: 3 W's of smartphone power consumption: Who, Where and How much is draining my battery?
authors: Agrim Gupta, Adel Heidari, Avyakta Kalipattapu, Ish Kumar Jain, Dinesh Bharadia
venue: ACM International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom)
why_needed: Per-component power measurement (using on-device power measurement hardware, not an estimated model) on real handsets, breaking phone battery drain down by subsystem including cellular and Wi-Fi radio activity. Supplies the measured energy cost of keeping a radio link active, which is the concrete number behind any claim that continuous participation drains a phone's battery, as opposed to an unmeasured assertion that it does.

title: Communication Latencies of Apple Push Notification Messages Relevant for Delivery of Time-Critical Information to Anesthesia Providers
authors: Richard H. Epstein, Franklin Dexter, Brian Rothman
why_needed: A four-month, 24-hour-a-day controlled measurement of Apple Push Notification Service delivery latency to real iOS devices over both Wi-Fi and cellular paths, sending one probe message per minute throughout. Reports mean latency under 100 seconds but a non-trivial fraction of days with at least one severely delayed delivery (up to 42% of days on the iPhone in this study's device sample). This is a primary-source measurement of the reliability of the push-based wake mechanism that a backgrounded phone depends on to be reachable at all, as opposed to the vendor's stated design intent for the service.
